We've investigated the emergent symmetries of the O(3) nonlinear sigma model, incorporating SU(2) spin and U(1) gauge field fluctuations, to study the properties of the Dirac spin liquid phase. Our two low-lying monopole excitations are dirac fermions, whose behavior is constrained by the Dirac constraint. These monopoles are associated with the breaking of U(1) gauge invariant physics, producing a tower of excitations that reflects this physical constraint. Our findings also reveal that the Brinkmann-Rindler lattice geometry leads to a one-to-one correspondence between the O(3) spin liquid and the Dirac spin liquid, based on the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration. Our research demonstrates that the O(3) spin liquid and the Dirac spin liquid phase possess the same physical properties, despite their distinct gauge symmetries, thus establishing these two systems as equivalent realizations of the same physical system.

We investigate the one-dimensional spin-1 $Z_3$ spin system with additional next-nearest neighbors, incorporating both a quantum $Z_3$ symmetry and a quantum $Z_6$ symmetry arising from the $Z_3$ symmetry's projective transport. Our aim is to explore the least amount of explicit $Z_3$ symmetry breaking required to transition from a many-body localized phase to a delocalized phase. We accomplish this using a variational method in the single-particle basis and also through a numerical study in a 100-site lattice at weak explicit breaking. The results from these two approaches align at small explicit breaking strengths. We discovered that increasing temporal lattice sites enhances the explicit breaking required to achieve the delocalized state, suggesting that the $Z_3$ symmetry may be spontaneously broken in the localized phase. Moreover, we found that the extent of $Z_6$ symmetry breaking is significantly more substantial in the localized phase than in the delocalized phase. This represents the first observed instance of a $Z_6$ symmetry being spontaneously broken.

To investigate the magnetic structure of the non-collinear order of Cr$_2$Al, we employed a Monte-Carlo simulation combined with a Metropolis algorithm. Our results indicate that Cr$_2$Al and Mn$_2$Au have identical magnetic configurations, with sublattices oriented 90 degrees relative to one another. Notably, the magnetic structure of Cr$_2$Al features the largest in-plane angle between ferromagnetic components, suggesting non-collinear complications could enhance magnetocrystalline interactions. Finite-size scaling of the transition temperature confirmed our findings and also revealed a lower critical temperature of 65 K for large systems, as well as an unstable non-collinear structure in the presence of an external magnetic field.

In a rarefied micro-flow under specific conditions, conventional models simulating gas dynamics encounter issues such as nonphysical transport and excessive energy dissipation. To address this, a new statistical representation, the $\nu u$-model, has been devised, combining a general macroscopic expression for gas velocity $u$ with the binary collision dynamics of particles governed by the Boltzmann equation, specifically through the violent event frequency $\nu$. This novel approach enables the accurate reproduction of thermal transpiration, mitigates unnecessary energy degradation, and accurately replicates fluid dynamics, as seen in the simulation of rarefied micro-flow involving gas mixing with superfluid helium.

Existing solutions to few-shot semantic parsing typically achieve exceptional results by leveraging large amounts of unsupervised data. Unfortunately, this approach is limited and can't be applied easily due to the considerable time and computational resources required. A newer strategy that shows promising results is by fine-tuning pre-trained language models, although it depends on having a dataset to calibrate the model's vocabulary and function mapping, which can itself require substantial annotation. To address these issues, we present a novel methodology and accompanying models that enable few-shot parsing even with minimal annotation by harnessing the power of unsupervised data and controlling model size and complexity. Specifically, we develop the Unsupervised SLU model, a streamlined sequence-to-sequence model, and the Unsupervised SLU Extension model, a robust sequence-to-sequence model, both of which outperform the existing state-of-the-art models according to formal Konversation and Semeval 2018 evaluation metrics. When testing with only 16 examples, our method demonstrated a remarkable 19.05% and 21.15% improvement in Konversation and Semeval 2018 scores, respectively. Moreover, the Unsupervised SLU model achieved scores comparable to the full training dataset model on the Semeval 2018 task 12 dataset and significantly outperformed it on the Konversation dataset, showcasing its exceptional few-shot performance.

We present findings from the testing of two innovative technologies - a Depleted Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor and a novel type of photodetector - both designed for advanced tracking systems. 

In-depth characterization of the sensors was carried out using particle beams at CERN's Square Kilometer Array Institute's demonstration facility and the Kyoto University's beam test facility, where researchers recorded data at high rates and high radiation levels.

Utilizing specialized readout circuits and advanced manufacturing techniques, these sensors effectively manage high readout rates and offer good performance even in harsh radiation environments. 

Feasibility studies for future particle physics experiments were also conducted, including investigations into the capabilities of the sensors to detect minimum ionizing particles, track reconstruction, and rate filtering. 

Based on the results, these sensors appear to be suitable for several current and future particle physics experiments, including the KOTO experiment, SHiP, the Square Kilometer Array, and the future Mu2e II experiment. 

Two research papers are referenced that provide further details on the sensors: "A Monolithic Sensor for Future Tracking Detectors" (arXiv:2106.14259) and "Characterization of a Novel Photodetector for the Square Kilometer Array" (arXiv:2106.14262).

Using a combination of XMM-Newton data, our study delves into the low-mass AGN 2XMM J123103.2+110648, involving multi-band photometry and spectroscopy analysis. 2XMM J123103.2+110648, at a redshift of 0.179, is one of the closest active galactic nuclei. Its extremely bright and fluctuating X-ray emissions are of great interest. Our XMM-Newton data yield a count rate of 2.24 plus/minus 0.15 counts per second across two separate observations. By fitting different models to the XMM-Newton X-ray spectrum, our analysis suggests a column density of 0.01 to 0.04 times 10 to the power of 22 per cubic centimeter. This range includes the host galaxy's column density but excludes any associated with a supermassive black hole. Our observations of the object in U, B, and R bands, along with a new ground-based spectroscopic measurement using the Doppler Spectral Range facility's Daedalus spectrometer on iSLEPT, show a redshift of 0.179, matching our prior X-ray-based finding. Furthermore, our measurements of B and U bands yield magnitudes of 17.090 and 16.029, respectively, along with a lack of any significant broad emission lines in our spectrum. Our data and analyses confirm the object to be a low-mass AG

The properties of the magnetospheres surrounding B-type magnetic stars, including their formation and composition, are not yet fully understood. To study these magnetospheres, researchers conducted an extensive survey of the Skymap spectrograph at the SOAR telescope, focusing on 10 magnetic early B-type stars with a specified surface magnetic field strength. Our investigation revealed a substantial increase (>1000%) in the number of suitable targets, resulting in the detection of new candidates along the Southern B-type magnetic Oe/Skymap project. Our high-resolution spectroscopic data showed that about 60% of these magnetospheres have a sub-keV gas temperature, 45% exhibit the presence of the wind from the star's surface, and 20% display the presence of a secondary ionized source. Our research further indicates that the magnetospheres surrounding these B-type stars have an average radial extent of 2.3±0.5 dipole radii. The observed properties of the magnetospheres are consistent with those generated by accretion from a compact, rapidly rotating companion star. In this compact system, the smaller component's radius could be as low as 0.1 R sun. Additionally, the accretion may be the result of a hydrodynamic instability that causes the smaller star's fast-rotating equator to lose its orbital momentum and transfer it to its slower polar regions. As a consequence, the accretion pattern shifts from regular stripes to delta-shaped formations.
A generalized form of intertwining operators is explored, with connections to oscillator operators in one dimension and Euclidean QFT remormalization.

We analyzed the spindle-shaped galaxies from a sample of isolated dwarf galaxies, using VLA data to measure H30α emissions and comparing them to Spitzer infrared data for star formation rate (SFR) calculations. To assess bias in SFR derived from radio H30α emissions versus infrared flux, we found H30α emissions generally overestimate SFR by about 0.2 dex compared to total infrared flux, a result similar to prior studies, possibly due to the distinct energy sources contributing to these emissions. We discovered that H30α emissions from normal galaxies have similar properties to those seen in ultrafaint dwarf galaxies, with their line flux scaling in relation to SFR and 100 micron luminosity, and also observed a 'cut-off' in radio emissions above a certain SFR threshold, potentially resulting in underestimated SFR if only radio emissions are considered. We further observed a near-proportional relationship between spin and SFR for these isolated galaxies, with higher SFRs correlated with greater angular momentum.

We demonstrate that for an infinite dihedral group, a free abelian group of rank 2, and certain virtually cyclic groups including a finitely generated torsion group, continuous minimal actions on compact Hausdorff spaces have a robust invariant. Specifically, we prove that these groups possess a distinct invariant under actions that are highly robust: equivalent to their original form after reduction by certain subgroups. Notably, we find that $\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1}{2}]\rtimes \mathbb{Z}$, a group representing a circle rotation followed by a mirror reflection, has the greatest possible level of robustness. In contrast, we show that a specific type of almost coherent permutation group, coercive permutation groups, which may have additional arbitrary properties, only possess a robust action that is essentially equivalent to one of its subgroup iterations. To achieve this, we first establish that a certain class of torsion groups, which may be infinitely generated, are virtually cocyclic. Furthermore, we expand our knowledge of virtually abelian groups by proving that a family of two-factorable groups, including finite abelian groups and certain finitely generated torsion groups, possess a robust action. Additionally, we resolve a long-standing open problem in the field by demonstrating that a specific type of torsion group, which may be infinitely generated, is virtually cocyclic.

This paper explores non-linear projection projection operators for time-dependent partial differential equations, focusing on the Poisson equation with non-local reaction. We examine the convergence properties of these operators, both in the context of classical projection operators, like Galerkin approaches, and kernel-based techniques, like collocation and interpolation, both with and without quadrature. We compare the latter, which includes methods like FEM, FPQ, FPQ2, QFEM, and QFPQ. We then analyze a quadrature-based kernel-based projection method, which we'd previously developed, in the context of the model equation. We combine this projection method with a temporal Petrov-Galerkin approach, using both standard and quadrature-based kernels, and discuss the resulting time-discrete equations, solving them using Rothe's method, which also applies quadrature, and providing error estimates, which we'd previously done in the context of classical projection methods, but now for the quadrature-based method. We apply these results to two concrete cases, splitting the time interval into sub-intervals, which we'd previously done for the one-dimensional heat equation, but now for the one-dimensional damped wave equation. We find that splitting reduces quadrature errors, which backs up numerical results.

This work develops and assesses an observer designed for high-precision state estimation in a class of complex, nonlinear systems, specifically large-scale mathematical models describing infectious disease spread. By leveraging a novel, two-part observer architecture, the proposed method achieves impressive state estimation accuracy using limited sensor data, available at fast update rates. To evaluate the observer's effectiveness, the researchers implemented a realistic simulation environment representing various real-world scenarios. Comprehensive numerical results illustrate the proposed observer's performance superiority over a widely used observer method from the literature. Additionally, the study highlights the significant advantages of the new observer approach over simulated sensors that incorporate noise, demonstrating its versatility in multiple complex simulation environments.

Knowledge graph embeddings have gained significant interest in the research community, focusing on representing entities and their relationships in a meaningful way. Various methods have been developed to achieve this, including real-space and embedding-space projection techniques. Real-space projection methods group all entities into clusters based on their similarity, mapping them into a lower-dimensional space, but do not consider the temporal aspect of relationships. Embding-space projection methods, on the other hand, learn neural network models to represent relationships and then project them into a lower-dimensional space, but are hindered by projection loss, which can distort the original embedding. To address these issues, a new method, TKG-Pro, addresses projecting knowledge graph embeddings by selecting important temporal relationships and grouping similar entities, leveraging clustering techniques to avoid projection loss. Experimental results on four knowledge graphs demonstrate that TKG-Pro outperforms existing projects, including those using neural network models, in multiple tasks.

We introduce a novel method for producing stable Kerr-lens mode-locking in ultra-short pulse lasers, incorporating an amplitude filter located outside the laser cavity. This innovative approach enables the generation of stable, secure seed pulses capable of surviving and initiating mode-locking within the laser itself. Utilizing our established setup, we achieved stable pulse generation with a pulse width of approximately 200 fs and a high peak power exceeding 5 watts. This configuration offers promising prospects for the development of advanced, ultra-high power pulse sources.

As the prevalence of edge devices and Internet of Things (IoT) devices grows, so does the concern for the energy efficiency of these devices. A recently developed technique, asynchronous online federated learning, has received consideration due to its potential to reduce energy consumption. Nonetheless, the common partial replication-based communication method used in this framework still consumes excess communication resources. To address this, we put forth a novel partial-sharing-based communication method that efficiently reduces communication overhead. Our method design includes two primary components. First, we establish a threshold for the amount of data to be sent, taking into consideration the receiver's bandwidth and the time it can spend on data processing. Second, we encode the data using a device-adaptive code to ensure that it can be safely transmitted between participants. Our method was evaluated under various real-world scenarios using real-world datasets, such as EMNIST and Cinic-10. Our test results show that, compared to the partial replication-based method, our proposed approach yields significant reductions in energy consumption, averaging an 0.46x and 0.32x decrease in energy consumption for EMNIST and Cinic-10, respectively, while also achieving enhanced accuracy. Our device-energy consumption model can be easily extended to support additional energy sources. Additionally, the proposed communication method is versatile and can be easily integrated with existing federated learning protocols, making it a suitable alternative.

We investigate and optimize a photodiode solid-state source operating at the TeP 4d transition at 25.84 nm. A novel approach using a thin silicon film inside a high-Q cavity formed by a photonic crystal and a mirror is described. For thicker silicon films, we demonstrate a switchable interaction between the source and the mirror's eigenfrequencies and a related modulation of optical absorption. Additionally, we identify a regime in which the source can operate independently of the mirror's resonance, preserving its properties. Furthermore, we propose combining strain and regenerative feedback techniques to enhance the source's sensitivity and stability. Ultimately, this setup may facilitate the development of high-sensitivity TeX-ray interferometers and quantum X-ray cats, laying the groundwork for innovative applications in X-ray quantum information processing and precision measurement.

The exponential map's dynamics in the complex plane are connected to specific complex functions involving infinite sums, which can be seen as extensions of complex hypergeometric functions. These functions come in two forms, involving the Gauss hypergeometric function or its more generalized forms. Certain unique properties make certain functions relevant to number theory, while others relate to the partition function or hypergeometric integrals. They also have ties to the behavior of Mittag-Leffler functions or their differential inverses. Further research is needed to understand the behavior of these functions near singular points.

This survey covers a diverse range of topics at the forefront of research in the theory of expansive expansions across various dimensions. It specifically concentrates on advanced concepts within combinatorial design and their implications for theoretical computer science. We will also examine multi-dimensional expansion and its applications, including generating random graphs and constructing large expansive networks. Furthermore, we will explore the current state of research in the field and outline multiple avenues for future investigation.

The electronic and magnetic properties of a single layer of GdInO3, obtained from thin slices of a bulk material, have been analyzed using a reconfigurable array of nanosized crystals. By studying the properties of these isolated layers, we are able to investigate how the magnetic coefficients of the material are influenced by the structural transformation from an orthorhombic to a tetragonal lattice arrangement. We have also observed the magnetic behavior of the individual layers and the way in which the magnetic coefficients are stabilized as the temperature is lowered. These findings are consistent with the bulk material's magnetic behavior. Further study of these individual layers will enable a more profound understanding of the magnetic coefficients and electronic structure of the bulk material.

Learning node representations in sparse networks poses a challenge, particularly due to the prevalence of zero-degree nodes resulting from the natural degradation of signals in such networks. We introduce a new perspective on representing sparse networks via folding low-degree nodes into the corresponding super-gaussian spaces. We develop the Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM) approach, which generalizes the Spectral Embedding (SE) method by folding zero-degree nodes and zero-degree neighborhoods into the super-gaussian spaces defined by the first H-order eigenvectors. We prove that SNHAM maintains the advantages of SE while rectifying its drawbacks in representing folded nodes. Empirical evaluations demonstrate SNHAM's superiority over SE and other competitive methods in representing sparse networks and conducting node classification tasks.

In a single-chamber pill system, the pill vapor density peaks too early and the pill activation process begins before the chamber is fully filled with vapor. This article presents a design modification to a pill geometry which can postpone the pill activation and improve the dose delivery rate. The proposed design divides the pill into two separate chambers, connected only through a small opening, thereby creating a stable environment for vapor pressure equilibrium between the two chambers, allowing the pill activation to be delayed until both chambers are fully filled with vapor. The pill design was tested using simulation tools, such as FLUENT for vapor flow and COMSOL for vapor and drug concentration inside the pill. The results showed an increase in the dose delivery rate by 26% and confirmed the efficacy of the proposed design through comparison with standard one-chamber pills.

Deep learning models of optical communication systems have greatly enhanced our understanding of the subject, allowing for accurate simulation and analysis of PM-RZ formats and their nonlinear interactions. However, prior studies primarily utilized machine learning approaches rooted in probabilistic models, such as Gaussian processes or mixture density networks. In our research, we introduce an innovative method for modeling optical communication systems, specifically nonlinear interference, by leveraging deep flow networks. This approach, grounded in physics-inspired machine learning, has been successfully applied to a specific scenario, PM-RZ differential phase-shift-keying with 2-pulse-position modulation, demonstrating excellent results in a realistic simulation environment. Our findings using this new model are corroborated by conventional method validations, including visual inspections, statistical tests, and comparisons with previous machine learning-based studies. Ultimately, we believe that physics-inspired methods like the one we've described hold great promise for the robust and reliable modeling of optical systems.

Image fusion technology has been widely applied to observe the earth's surface simultaneously, and it plays a significant role in monitoring wildfires. Current deep learning-based image fusion techniques exhibit superior performance in fused images, yet they lack assessment via established metrics in the field. In contrast, traditional image fusion approaches utilize specific metrics to evaluate and optimize the fusion process. This research applies established metrics to assess the performance of four cutting-edge image fusion deep learning methods. The findings reveal that certain established metrics can efficiently evaluate the performance of deep learning-based image fusion techniques. Moreover, the study showcases the effectiveness of deep learning-based image fusion methods over traditional approaches by creating an artificial fire dataset and real-fire imagery extracted from National Wildland-Coastal Fire Detection System data. The analysis also examines the impact of diversifying training datasets on the performance of deep learning-based image fusion models. The research data, including the artificial fire dataset and implementation codes, are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/111111111Nn/Near.

Diagnosing mental health using a physical examination is challenging as it relies heavily on symptoms that can be seen or measured, overlooking those that aren't visible. Social media has recently emerged as a tool for mental health diagnosis, leveraging users' expressed feelings and behaviors. By merging clinical knowledge from physical examinations with the social media's unique insights, a comprehensive diagnosis can be made. Just like physical examinations, a thorough social media investigation is crucial in pinpointing mental health. Current methods, however, struggle to offer an in-depth assessment, often relying on explicit user confession or informal polls. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage procedure for mental health diagnosis that incorporates social media observations of daily behaviors, such as how users interact with content, including conversations online. Our research also demonstrates that social media-borne mental health diagnosis can be just as accurate as physical examinations, providing substantial evidence to support its utilization in mental health diagnosis and treatment.

The novel coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, has become a global public health threat due to its high infectivity and significant mortality rate, as depicted in widely publicized graphs showing an exponential growth pattern of confirmed cases and fatalities across the globe, with the international case count surpassing 15 million and over a million fatalities as of December 2021. The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has become a pivotal concern for the global community. In an effort to curb the spread of the disease, most countries have implemented temporary lockdowns, suspending social activities for an indefinite period, while also leading to an immense economic downturn. In light of these challenges, the primary goal of this study is to introduce a two-layer epidemic model that incorporates the effects of hospitals and health care institutions on the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic, in combination with lockdown measures. By applying the comparison principle, the qualitative properties of the model are established, including the existence and stability of the steady points, as well as the long-term behavior of the model. Furthermore, the study develops and applies a numerical algorithm for approximating the model's solution, as well as the approximate time it takes for the population to recover from the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic. In addition, the study conducts two numerical case studies using data from the United States, focusing on the southern region, which recorded over 3.3 million cases and 40,000+ fatalities as of December 2021, as well as other

The interaction between the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) and the Isoscalar Giant Quadrupole Resonance (ISGQR) in deformed nuclei affects their respective energy levels and widths. Calculations using a microscopic transport theory and the Hartree-Fock-RPA (Random Phase Approximation) model show that the ISGMR and ISGQR coupled to the one-photon one-hole excitations have lower energy peaks than the unperturbed configurations. Additionally, the width of the ground state branch was observed to be around 4 MeV. The position of the ISGMR dip after coupling was found to be lower than the uncoupled level, corresponding to a density variation of $\Delta\rho=-0.12$ fm$^{-3}$. The ISGQR coupled to the neutron-proton interaction showed a smaller density variation of $\Delta\rho=-0.07$ fm$^{-3}$. The calculated density variations are in agreement with the predictions made using the folding model.

This paper explores the stochastic dynamics of a microelectromechanical system called a micro-resonator under the influence of a variable spring constant. The non-sticky portion of the micro-resonator is actuated by a position-based feedback loop. To model its dynamics, a combination of the Landau-Ginzburg equation and the Kelvin-Voigt model is used for the free part, while a modified Frenkel-Klingenberg model is employed for the stuck region. The paper's key contributions involve identifying key parameters, establishing primary states, and providing main state identifications through a novel sliding motion approach. The results can be useful for analyzing micro-resonator dynamics during the development of new devices.

The efficiency of market trading is impacted by various factors such as costs, network effects, and constraints, which are especially prevalent in markets with small capitalization. A multi-agent trading platform was developed to model market dynamics and investigate the effectiveness of different strategies. A novel reinforcement learning approach, involving policy gradient estimation, was employed to tackle the non-markovian nature of the problem. Which two learning methods were utilized in the experiment and how do they differ in their treatment of state variables?

Understanding user intent is vital for providing personalized experiences and optimizing the user experience in various systems. This study introduces a new neural network framework called MARS, which learns a multi-aspect response space to model user intent. By incorporating multiple inputs, MARS captures a broad range of user motivations and demonstrates the ability to uncover a variety of intentional factors through exploration. Based on this exploration, MARS generates an array of possible intents and selects a single index to produce a personalized recommendation. Our evaluation of MARS is conducted using a real dataset from a leading Chinese e-commerce recommendation platform and the results demonstrate its superiority over existing approaches.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation can be simplified into a Bessel equation under specific relationships between its parameters. Specifically, if specific parameter relationships are met, namely $k+\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}-(-m-k-{\frac{1}{2}}\epsilon^{-1})$, $(m,k)$ being non-negative integers and $\epsilon$ being small, then a nearly Askey--Wilson limit arises. In this nearly limit $k+\frac{1}{2}$ serves as a large parameter. The focus here is on when the nearly limit nearly approaches a holomorphic solution in the almost entire complex plane except for the origin. The conditions under which this nearly limit nearly approaches a holomorphic solution are related to the behavior of a Bessel function of the second kind of order $2k+1$, where this function must be holomorphically continuable in the entire complex plane except for the origin. The requirements for this nearly limit nearly approaches a holomorphic solution thus arise.

A key capability of principal component analysis (PCA) is its ability to recover a smooth matrix of low rank as input. A recent study combines PCA with weighted combinations and finds that PCA remains effective even when the weights are smoothly changing, using an adapted metric that measures performance on the manifold of p-schatten norms. The study shows that PCA remains an optimal method when the weights are on the PCA manifold, using the p=2 case as an example of optimality. The study also analyzes a geometrically-structured problem and finds that PCA performs well even with significant Gaussian noise, with numerical verifications supporting the findings. The study concludes by examining the performance of PCA in a neural network designed to recover low-rank matrices, finding that PCA is a robust and efficient method due to its optimality and role in feature extraction, selection, and projection. A numerical investigation supports these findings and highlights PCA's efficiency and adaptability.

Systems with suppressed boundary interactions form the foundation for numerous research in quantum systems, yet this idea is also significantly broader in scope, impacting classical systems as well. In fact, systems without boundary symmetry can still exhibit fractional boundary states, which are exemplified by fractional skylines and ring systems discussed here. These classical mechanisms may also underlie phenomena seen in quantum Hall and Dirac cone edges, making their study important for both quantum and classical theories.

This paper introduces an adaptive distributed controller for linear continuous-time systems, capable of maintaining functionality in the face of unexpected events. Building upon the theoretical framework of networked system dynamics, its key components are informed by the principles of swarm intelligence, Bass' algorithm, and adaptive dynamics. Consequently, the controller exhibits stable, resilient properties, and its application in fluid mixing within a rotating continuous-time system demonstrates the practical benefits of this innovative approach.

This study presents an effective deep learning-based solution to address the challenging task of deriving retinal fluid from Fluorescein Angiography (FA) images. Our two-phase framework combines a generative adversarial denoising component followed by a retinal fluid identification algorithm. Retinal fluid detection is formulated as a multi-class problem, where we evaluated three approaches: reducing dimensionality, incorporating spatial data, and using attention mechanisms. Our experiment's focus was on assessing the performance of different techniques combined with a powerful attention-based model. Ultimately, our framework achieved impressive results, securing a 0.903 mean average precision on our validation dataset and earning a score of 0.871 on the test dataset in the DERFI challenge.

The widespread occurrence of complex networks in both natural and engineered systems demands a profound understanding of their fundamental principles. In our research, we've compiled a collection of analytical tools for exploring the relationship between networks and their underlying dynamics, consisting of approximately 650 pages and roughly 2000 formulas. This comprehensive toolbox spans topics such as network construction, dynamic models, linear stability analysis, and multifractal characterization, while also incorporating relevant computational methods. In addition to its practical value as a practical guide, this document provides an in-depth review of the numerical and mathematical aspects related to network dynamics, which has been historically underemphasized in scientific literature. As such, we've strived to incorporate both the latest discoveries in the field and a dose of practical realism, while also enabling seamless extensions and modifications whenever necessary. Ultimately, we're confident that this toolbox will serve as a versatile platform for both seasoned professionals and newcomers to further investigate the intricate and multifaceted realm of complex networks.

Our research proposes an innovative framework that intersects evolutionary theory and ecological studies, aiming to broaden our understanding of the interplay between these processes through a novel quantitative approach. By leveraging a flexible statistical tool, we conduct an extensive analysis of the underlying trends within numerous biological datasets, uncovering patterns that can be explained by the sensitivity of living organisms to temperature and mutation. The core of our framework comprises two connected dynamic models, one governing the diverse dynamics of ecosystems and the other focusing on adaptive evolutionary processes. These models consistently yield comparable expressions that can be directly linked, enabling us to derive a precise mathematical equation that relates to the inherent rate of evolution, the width of its underlying distribution, and the level of ecological instability. Additionally, our framework predicts that there should be a noticeable increase in the diversity of species within areas with high levels of ecological complexity, an idea supported by numerous studies in various fields.

Previous studies on the security of speech representation models have mainly focused on defenses against unsavory adversaries. However, it's unclear how these models perform against more sophisticated attackers, such as those with various degrees of information or motivation. This research delves into the robustness of speech representation models against three types of attacks: one in which the adversary has no prior knowledge, one that's informed but lacks motivation for malice, and one that's both knowledgeable and intent on causing harm. Using a range of benchmark datasets and adversary models, the study evaluates the robustness of speech representation models against targeted attacks and reveals notable vulnerabilities. Specifically, the experiments involving adversarial attacks on PLP and MFCC features have shown that modestly increased attack scales can completely erase target information from these features. Consequently, the framework's ability to leverage these features is severely impaired. Moreover, the attacks aimed at the speech representation models' embedding and codebook spaces show that even brief access to these spaces enables an adversary to manipulate the models and specifically target embedded data. The attacks also highlight the PLP domain's vulnerability to generalizable attacks. To address these concerns, the study proposes a simple challenge-and-respond CAPTCHA system designed to prevent unauthorized access to the model's feature space. Experimentally, the results demonstrate that while users with knowledge of the challenge respond correctly, adversaries without prior information are unable to solve the challenge and consequently cannot carry out the attack. Consequently, the study concludes that incorporating a simple yet effective CAPTCHA system

Arbitrage opportunities in Automated Market Makers (AMMs) on crypto exchanges are often assessed with the Total Variance Method, however this paper demonstrates the efficacy of this approach is questionable. We develop a theoretical framework to analyze the properties of AMM pricing curves and demonstrate that in an optimal AMM operation, an oscillating (concave or convex) pricing curve is favored. This is because a certain type of curvature can boost contributors' gains and also make it easier to achieve fairness. The study also shows that in the best possible AMM operation, the risk can be reduced by creating a curve with (convex or concave) incline. We go on to demonstrate that the relationship between risk and contributors' gains is not accurately captured by the Total Variance Method, and that a more suitable metric for assessing risk is the Asymmetric Mean Absolute Deviation (AMAD) metric. This paper supports earlier research by Seward et al. (2021) that partially discovered this relationship, and our work showcases a broader applicability of the AMAD metric in AMM evaluation.

Causal conclusions rely heavily on data, yet dealing with missing data poses further complications, making it challenging to trust the identified cause-effect relationships. As the issue of estimating causal relationships from incomplete data is a statistical problem, we propose a solution by utilizing the multiplex neural network for multiple imputation. This study evaluates the efficacy of this approach using both synthetic and real-world finite sample datasets. Specifically, we utilize the multiplex neural network, previously known as "Occhio," a more advanced model, for imputation procedures. Multiple imputation techniques involve reconstructing the data distribution of the completely observed sample, and recent developments demonstrate that this is achievable with high success rates using deep neural networks. We introduce the E-value, a measure of robustness for causal conclusions concerning missing data, and compare the performance of the robustness of the causal conclusions with those obtained from various multiple imputation methods. We conduct an in-depth analysis of simulated data as well as a real-world examination using patients' sleep patterns, as recorded across multiple sessions, a problem characterized by the presence of a large number of missing values. We demonstrate that the E-value allows for the evaluation of the reliability of the inferred cause-effect relationships, and we further observe that the multiplex neural network yields robust estimates, competing favorably with other multiple imputation methods.

The U_q(U(sl_2)) symmetries are examined in detail, specifically those that exist on the level of wave functions, where several distinct types are identified. These types are characterized by how they relate to Fock spaces and Fock modules, with particular focus on scalar transformations and their connections to the q-exponential function. Ultimately, an in-depth analysis concludes that there are essentially two major categories of U_q(U(sl_2)) symmetries: one that remains intact after transformation and another that is reversed. Key relationships between these categories are proven, with special attention to potential ambiguities arising from quantum lattices and irreducible representations. A comprehensive review of previous work and the current state of theory are also provided.

The integration of Blockchain technology into Internet of Vehicles (IoV) has been suggested as a way to enhance stability and security. Nevertheless, customary smart contract design for IoV may compromise data security and privacy. In this paper, we present a new approach to designing a smart contract using a zero-knowledge proof system for unverified vehicles to interact securely with roadside infrastructure without sharing their private information. We introduce a concept called "functor" as a way to protect high-level data descriptions and use them to create specific gradient-based proof of ownership for road conditions, as an example of how functors can be used. We propose a framework, called VZKSF, for making proofs about a vehicle's state through a process of query, update, and proof, as a way to use proof systems more efficiently. We also introduce a concept called the "obfuscator" as a way to protect a vehicle's state when it is used with proof systems, as a way to optimize proof generation and improve the scalability of proof systems.

A precise examination is made of heavy quark quark hadronization processes, leveraging the form factors driving these reactions. Utilizing a four-vector collider experiment with beauty quarks and a theoretical model that accounts for all possible quark and gluon states, a proportion of beauty quarks is found to undergo hadronization with strange mesons, with this ratio measured and compared to a prior similar investigation involving charm quarks.

A cryogenic microwave laboratory is being developed for experiments with cold gases and ultra-cold gases. The experimental setup, spanning ~60cm in length, ~40cm in width, and ~60cm in height, will have remote temperature control capabilities, ranging from 4K to 50mK. The platform incorporates microwave resources, including a spectrometer capable of producing and detecting entangled photon pairs at ~3-15 GHz, and a magnet with a variable field of up to 10 Tesla. The platform's microwave resources can be moved, oriented, and combined in multiple configurations to meet the demands of varying experiments. The platform's temperature and communication systems, including fiber infrastructure, are also being implemented to support these experiments.

Due to the prevalent misuse of cryptography in software applications, researchers employed middle school students as "users-in-the-wild" to evaluate the human factor in software design. Conducting a survey of 75 individuals via a crowdfunding platform, the study discovered that students from diverse backgrounds who had no prior knowledge in cryptography were engaged to design API's for a cryptocurrency library, contrasting common programming languages such as Java and C. The results indicated that the inherent characteristics of Python, which has fluent string manipulation and frequent function reuse, contributes to an increased likelihood of developers misusing crypto functions compared to Java and C. Furthermore, the study found that string-based functions and those with unusual names frequently led to the misuse of their respective crypto functions. Additionally, users-in-the-wild displayed ambiguity in determining the purpose of a crypto function when it has multiple related meanings, suggesting that clear and concise function naming can reduce the likelihood of misuse. Lastly, the study found that internal comments within code can fail to provide insight into the proper utilization of a crypto function, whereas external documentation is viewed as more trustworthy. Thus, the study proposes that effective anti-abuse measures for cryptography should not only target software developers but also the broader community of crypto users.

Three-dimensional image reconstruction from two-dimensional scans like images or histograms is a basic problem in statistics and machine learning, and a long-standing question revolves around the optimal size of the two-dimensional data set needed to produce reliable three-dimensional information, especially when dealing with large data. A significant obstacle in addressing this question arises from the conflicting requirements of sufficient three-dimensional data for reliable results and the limited quality of recovered three-dimensional information due to small data sets. A new method we developed overcomes this challenge by providing an objective way to evaluate the quality of recovered three-dimensional data, allowing us to answer the standing question and revealing that the quality of recovered data rapidly improves with data size, and that the basic principles of our method are applicable to a broad range of large-scale imaging and reconstruction applications. An important area where our work is relevant is large-scale 3D image and sound data analysis, encompassing not only physical scan data but also vast digital archives and computational reconstruction of data. Examples of such data include high-resolution MRI scans, video, and sound tracks. A related field where our work is relevant is the numerical analysis of massive two-dimensional data sets, including vast archives of documents and images, and segments of data where human quality control is impossible. A related area where our work is relevant is the numerical analysis of massive two-dimensional data sets, including vast archives of documents and images, and segments of data where human quality control is impossible.

A time-reversal-based method is developed for the accurate extraction of sparse coefficients representing reflectivity within a subsurface. By extending a two-dimensional sparse modeling approach to one dimension, the proposed method synthesizes nonuniform, non-convex wavefield samples across depths. This allows for a more effective recovery of time-reversal-based subsurface reflection coefficients, even in cases where the extraction process is hampered by significant background noise. Numerical simulations that mimic real-life seismic acquisition scenarios validate the efficacy of our novel method by demonstrating its superior performance relative to the classical sparse modeling technique. Additionally, the model assumes that unmodeled features such as direct and multiply scattered waves do not significantly impact the recovery of the subsurface model.

we've demonstrated that the relation $\|T_g\|_{BMOA_p} \leq C\|T_g\|_{BMOA_{p_0}}$ 
holds for $1 < p_0 < 2$, where $T_g = R_g f$ for some function $f$ on the manifold. 
It was also proven that the compactness of $T_g$ to $BMOA_p$ for $1 < p < 2$ 
implies the compactness of $T_g$ to $BMOA_{p_0}$. This enables the following to be established: 
$T_g$ is compact from $BMOA_2$ to itself if, and only if, it is compact from $BMOA_{1.5}$

and $\|R_g f\|_{BMOA_{p_0}}$, it was found that the compactness of $T_g$ to $BMOA_p$

We've developed a novel, versatile method for determining the conformal data of quantum spin chains that utilizes high-energy collisions between solitons. Our method applies a unitary transformation to the original Hamiltonian, switching to a new Hilbert space where the Hamiltonian is no longer a thorough description of the system's dynamics. Instead, we can use the new space's Hamiltonian to identify key properties of the solitons and their interactions. Our method leverages the solitons' unique characteristics to simplify the complicated interactions, allowing us to compute the conformal data and other properties, such as soliton masses, form factors, and anomalous dimensions, using our overarching approach. We've successfully demonstrated this approach's effectiveness for a range of well-known quantum spin chains, including the XX, XXX, XYY, and isotropic XY models. Our calculations are analytical and accurate. Our method isn't limited to these models, and we anticipate it will be applied to studying more intricate systems, such as those with many solitons and complicated interactions.

Traditional sequence-to-sequence models have limitations when dealing with unknown words in sequence labeling tasks like part-of-speech tagging. To overcome this challenge, our proposed set-valued prediction method allows for more accurate outputs by taking into account the possible set of relevant labels instead of predicting a single label for each word. Our experiments with part-of-speech tagging on the Penn Treebank dataset reveal that the set-valued approach yields comparable performance with existing state-of-the-art models across various word types, including common and uncommon words. Interestingly, our method achieves this level of performance without incorporating additional loss terms or regularization, simply by incorporating set-valued predictions in the model. To facilitate research in this area, our code will be made publicly available on the GitHub platform.

To determine if a sequence of non-decreasing, continuous functions converges to another limit function, we must first identify if the limit function can be correctly determined and then establish its properties. In the context of sequences of demand functions, we must also establish the characteristics of the limit function under various conditions, such as converging sequences of sequences of prices and quantities, and sequences of partial derivatives, all while accounting for possible infinitesimal jumps. Our results allow for our approach to be applied in a wide range of economic applications, including sequences of non-atomic demand functions, and both exogenous and endogenous sequences of prices. Our methodology also enables the handling of more general topological spaces, such as locally convex topological vector spaces, and Banach spaces. Our work extends the existing contributions of Topsoe, Alspach and Brown, and provides a comparison of our approach with their work. Our final chapter also examines the conditions under which the sequence of sequences of partial derivatives converges to the partial derivative of the limit function, and highlights its applicability in general equilibrium theory, particularly in the context of sequences of subdifferentials in commodity and factor price spaces.

In smart city monitoring systems, the performance of system components often relies on non-techical natural language-based metrics such as energy consumption, water consumption, or traffic status. The specifications of these metrics can be ambiguous or prone to inaccuracies, which can be addressed by leveraging formal methods based on formalizable ontologies. An ontology formalizing monitoring data analysis can help verify system performance against non-techical, imprecise or vague metrics, as well as transform these metrics into unambiguous logical formulas. This paper focuses on a particular smart city monitoring system called Smart City Sensors, which employs an ontology to translate non-techical metrics into formal logical formulas. Our approach utilizes formalization to analyze imprecise or vague metrics, as well as automatic proof techniques to verify system performance against these metrics. Our main contribution lies in the application of formal methods to monitor smart cities, as well as the integration of semantic translation of imprecise metrics into formal logical formulas.

A recent study proposes a new approach to mitigate effects of noise in quantum systems by targeting specific angular momentum properties in variational quantum eigensolver algorithm. It demonstrates that this technique can be implemented without substantial increases in qubit count, specifically by adding an angular momentum gate for each harmonic oscillator state. It is rigorously proven that this scheme can control the error exponential growth caused by noise and maintain a constant overlap between quantum states. Numerical simulations show the scheme's effectiveness in reducing variations in matrix element estimates, thereby converging faster to the target energy eigenstate. Notably, an approximately 60% improvement in VQE convergence rate can be achieved with limited qubit extra cost. Additionally, the scheme's scalability is further assessed using a IBM quantum device and real-world H$_2$ molecule systems.

In a particular type of category called n-permutable regular categories, which encompass various categories including categories of sets, these categories have properties that allow certain types of objects and morphisms to behave well with suprema and infima. By testing the properties of objects and morphisms regarding their interaction with suprema and infima, it is possible to determine the existence of certain objects and morphisms, such as cartesian images and suprema of chains. In the case of topos, these properties can be decided by checking the properties of a family of object known as the family factorization system. This same method can be applied to a broader category of pre-regular categories, which include n-permutable regular categories, by identifying a certain family of object known as the regular factorization system. In addition to these decisions, it is also possible to decide on certain properties of these systems, such as decidability of (n-1)-permutable. In the case of a particular type of category called 1-permutable regular category, which can be considered a subset of pre-regular categories, these decisions can be made by checking the properties of a family of object known as the regular Eilenberg-Mac Lane objects. All these decisions can be made by a category with suprema of chains through a decidable method, which can also decide whether a particular type of system, known as the n-permutation property, holds true.

This study utilizes high-resolution satellite imagery to track waves in the North East Atlantic. Satellite imagery is merged with in-situ wind speed data from the BuOYE wind buoy to create a distance-based reference system. An extreme value theory-based model is then constructed, conditioning on extremely high Metop wind speeds to study wave patterns. By doing so, it finds that very high waves and winds exhibit similar patterns, with spatial decay approximately following a Gaussian process with a standard deviation of about 500 to 1000 kilometers. This model is able to forecast more severe waves following extremely high winds, matching observed wave patterns. An animation of the simulation, combining Metop wind speeds and BuOYE wave measurements, clearly shows this relationship, revealing wave patterns.

Within the realm of visual-language pre-training, a current area of focus lies in developing cross-modal retrieval systems that can learn visual and language representations equally well. This research introduces a novel, two-stage model for cross-modal retrieval, utilizing a large dataset with 9 million image-text pairs. The first stage enhances CLIP with visually-guided texts, leveraging a massive dataset of 1.4 billion image tags to refine text representations and boost text-image correlation. The second stage leverages VisCLIP's visuolinguistic context to refine text embeddings, thereby improving the efficiency of retrieving relevant images via concise, tag-based queries. When evaluated on MS-Coco, MS-MSKR, and Visual Genome, VCLIP consistently outperforms the current state-of-the-art models, both in visual recognition tasks and cross-modal retrieval tasks. Additionally, it demonstrates substantial efficiency improvements, with a 5-fold reduction in computational requirements compared to the top-performing models. The source code and datasets will be publicly released.

In the field of matrix calibration, inverse estimation, and alignment, a common task called shift alignment is performed on data matrices. Various methods for this task have been developed in applications across the sciences, including neuroscience and computer vision. A popular method called shift-dimensionality reduction, utilizing the nearest point approach, has been a staple in the field. However, a different method, proposing an optimal direction for rotation alignment, has been a key component in the field of computer vision. This method assumes a symmetric noise condition and proposes a different optimal shift direction, which differs from the nearest point approach. Interestingly, when noise asymmetry occurs, the proposed optimal shift direction is not just any arbitrary variant, but rather one that is specifically oriented towards capturing the principal component of the data.

By linking Mackey functors over odd primes to certain properties of stable homotopy groups, our work offers a novel approach that broadens the scope of Mackey functors beyond their initial applications in permutation group theory. Specifically, we've established a range of new Mackey functors associated with specific homotopy types, such as integral Morava K-theory and some form of Brown-Kervaire local conjugate map functors. Moreover, our new constructions align with the congruence data generated by the leading terms within Adams spectral sequences for some form of Brown-Kervaire local conjugate map functors, demonstrating their natural fit within the framework of modern homotopy theory.

We established in our previous work that for any ideal $I$ and a given module $M$ over a generalized power series ring, the $I$-stratification of the module $M$ directly corresponds to the $I$-stratification of the module $H_I^0(M)$. This realization led us to investigate generalized $I$-stratification for local cohomology modules, and we discovered a significant connection between the zero submodule of local cohomology and the function that governs the $F$-rationality of a local ring. We then used these findings to derive new approaches for achieving direct maximality and idealizer positivity. Furthermore, our work allows for the determination of specific, narrow intervals containing the plus class in the direction of the monoid of positive powers of the principal ideal $I$, especially in relation to local Lyubeznik numbers.

The growing applications of machine learning in medicine have created new complexities for team collaborations, including varied data formats and disparate software tools. A key issue arises when developing and using machine learning models in medicine, mainly due to the inability of models to share knowledge across different programming languages and architectures. To address this challenge, a new Python library called highdicom has been introduced, which aims to streamline the process of working with high-resolution medical images by providing a straightforward and efficient way to access image data. By using the HIDS protocol, which supports the large-scale transfer of data, highdicom facilitates the easy integration with various machine learning frameworks, including TensorFlow, Keras, and PyTorch. As a demonstration of the versatility of highdicom, we have successfully modified a pre-trained National Cancer Institute Advanced Clinical Architecture for Image Guided Surgery (IAGIS) model to run on a large dataset of CT scans using the HIDS, which allows for efficient transfer of data from an image server and enables the model to predict binary lesions confidently within a 2-centimeter radius. The highdicom library is available at https://github.com/mdtteam/highdicom.

The effect of diffeomorphisms on horizon structures is a crucial aspect of general relativity, particularly in the study of gravitational systems surrounding black holes and cosmological horizons. The key feature of the no-hair theorem in charged black holes is the invariance of the horizon structure, and how diffeomorphisms maintain this invariance is investigated. By imposing certain conditions on the Einstein equations and the gauge field equations, our first result demonstrates that the Hamiltonian for diffeomorphisms that preserve the horizon event horizon and for static horizons that maintain the horizon's causal structure are finite. We demonstrate through mathematical examples that our results are consistent across various types of horizons including Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordstrom, de Sitter, anti-de Sitter, and negative mass square horizons. By extrapolating our findings, our results are shown to be applicable to more complex systems such as charged black holes in a negative mass square space-time, brane cosmology, and loop quantum gravity. The total energy of a charged particle is also calculated, and our results are verified to hold true for both classical and quantized systems.

A novel method of bioprotein domain identification through deep learning is introduced in this study, along with an experimental validation of a related DNA classification model using the splice protein dataset. The proposed DNA classification model employs a sequential attention mechanism to prioritize critical positional features when classifying sequences. Experimental results show that the model achieves an accuracy of 85.9% on the test dataset, accuracy that complements and expands existing scientific knowledge regarding DNA sequences. Conversely, the associated protein domain identification model did not surpass the performance of existing state-of-the-art models using the SPSS dataset. Moreover, the learned splice signatures suggest the presence of specific positional and functional patterns in DNA codes, serving as foundational insights for future biological studies and potentially as metadata for analyzing DNA sequences. Finally, the proposed model's efficacy is assessed through a thorough examination of its reliability, highlighting the effectiveness of the splice protein dataset for training neural networks that can process protein sequences of varying lengths.

We analyze the spectral weight distribution in the Anderson model at low energy levels near the metal-insulator transition point. Using numerical methods to solve the model equations shows that the transition is characterized by the breakdown of a spectral weight sum rule. This finding implies that the metal-insulator transition in strongly correlated systems, like the Anderson model, is also marked by the collapse of an additional spectral weight sum rule. This discovery is consistent with our previous research on this model, as well as our current study on another model, the Hubbard model, which shows a similar pattern. Both models exhibit symptoms reminiscent of a quantum phase transition, which is further evidence that the transition is non-trivial. This conclusion is independent of whether or not the system has symmetrical wave function properties. Furthermore, the evidence suggests that the symmetry properties of the wave functions are not consistently reported across different levels of disorder strength. This finding is an important observation as it relates to systems that undergo a transition when interacting with an external bath of electrons, such as doped graphene, which also exhibits similar behavior.

We introduce a new method for developing symplectic integrators in multi-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian systems that leverage Lie-Poisson geometry. By partitioning the coadjoint orbit and representing the resulting constraints through collective variables, we create high-order integrators capable of preserving the coadjoint orbit, Casimirs, and kinetic energy. This method applies to a broad class of Lie-Poisson systems, including those describing the dynamics of skew-symmetric matrices and their generalizations. We implement this approach for numerical simulations in two techniques: running a collective map and combining individual integrators, both of which achieve high precision while preserving key invariants. We evaluate the precision and numerical invariants of our new integrators through numerical simulations of systems representing modified rigid body dynamics with a free wheel.

To evaluate the detection efficiency of planets in a future ground-based microlensing survey, we examine the effectiveness of various methods to identify planets through their perturbations of the microlensing point trajectory. We compare the ability of human experts and an autonomous neural network to detect these perturbations in a large dataset of light curves generated by the Galactic Bulge Microlensing Survey. By integrating these techniques, we estimate the efficiency of identifying planets with distinct characteristics, including the methods used to uncover previously unknown objects within the survey's previously analyzed data.

We create a novel approach to solving implicitly formulated approximations for conservation laws, involving an initial value problem in one spatial dimension. This method integrates viscous splitting in conjunction with a smooth viscosities strategy, and is specifically designed to align with discontinuity locations. By meticulously handling the resulting time-dependent diffusion equation, we derive a strict proof for the method's stability, utilizing the maximum principle. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we apply the method to challenging test cases.

The preemption of non-performing loans is a significant concern for the banking sector of developing countries, including South Africa. In this study, a comparison of different machine learning models, specifically gradient boosting, multilayer perceptron, random forest, and support vector machine, was made to determine which one performed best in predicting non-performing loans in South African banks, using data from the Periodic Reporting System database provided by the South African Reserve Bank. The research found that a gradient boosting model, with considerations for handling imbalances in the data, achieved high accuracy and precision in predicting non-performing loans. It also considered using secondary data from financial statements and credit applications to improve the predictions. Notably, the study highlighted that these models could potentially be integrated with financial screening tools to provide more informed decisions in the banking sector. Additionally, the research found that models could be tailored to specific risk types, such as default, foreclosure, and liquidation, and that collaboration between banks and regulators could lead to the development of more effective early warning systems for detecting problem loans.

We have discovered novel identities, involving the $q$-hit numbers and elementary symmetric functions, that can be expressed as the $q$-analogues of chromatic symmetric functions. These identities serve as the $q$-analogue of the famous Jacobi-Steffensen inequality and the $q$-analogue of the Stanley-MacDonald identity. Additionally, our work reveals the central role that certain $q$-analogues of chromatic symmetric functions play in the representation theory of the quantized special linear algebra. Utilizing the free fermion field theory, we are able to prove our results, which generalize well-known results in the ungraded quantum linear Schur-Weyl duality.

Image representations based on Gabor filters capture local image patterns and have proven effective across various visual tasks. However, the traditional approach to Gabor filters is lacking in robustness, as small orientation changes result in significantly different image representations. To address this limitation, we propose Landmark Gabor Filters, which pinpoint and amplify image features invariant to orientation. LGFs achieve this through three key mechanisms: (i) accurately localizing image patterns, (ii) amplifying desired signal while diminishing secondary cues, and (iii) enhancing the robustness of image representations to orientation changes. When integrated with self-supervised learning techniques, our method produces remarkable results in both closed-set and open-set proximal classification tasks, showcasing its potential for real-world applications. Additionally, our method's robustness is highlighted by its superior performance across various benchmark datasets.

The relative fundamental lemma has crucial applications in the local functional equations of L-functions and the study of endoscopic gluing in character identities, as demonstrated in the work of Ben Green, James Maynard, and Thomas Tinelli. This fundamental lemma implies a key conclusion: the sum of two orbital integrals evaluated on group elements is equal to a twisted orbital integral. The proof in existing literature relies on the smooth hasweh derivative, a concept challenging to apply in more complex scenarios. The current article addresses this limitation by establishing a comparable orbital integral theorem in the context of unitary groups. The proof in this work does not rely on the smooth hasweh derivative and is based on the concept of dual relative hasweh derivatives. Additionally, this proof is more transparent and accessible than previous implementations.

In a previous study, the impact of heavy quark mass corrections on the QCD evolution of parton distribution functions, specifically at third-order accuracy, was investigated, focusing on flavor changes. This work built upon previous two-loop findings, incorporating more complex numerical coefficients and allowing for non-zero mass differences between heavy and lighter quarks. The research considered the possibility of imaginary mass values for the heavier quark, which led to novel results, including those for charm and up/down or charm and strange quark flavor combinations. The calculations were performed using a momentum-space representation, ensuring a seamless integration with parton distribution functions and their straightforward application in various physical processes.

A sublinear time, almost linear time (ignoring small aspects) algorithm is proposed to verify whether a given graph G can be 2-edge-colored. The colored version of G must satisfy a degree discrepancy condition where the number of edges in G with degree d is always d or d minus 1. Our approach analyzes each edge of a given G approximation approximately, for an estimated O~{|E|^3/4|V|^{7/3}} time duration. We achieve this by first identifying a minimal subset of edges with inconsistent degree discrepancies. If a general graph G with a specific degree k has multiple types of edges with discrepancies of k and k minus 1, and if we consider a smaller graph G' obtained by removing a single edge, then G' will also have the same property of having multiple types of edges with discrepancies of k and k minus 1. We achieve our algorithm by first reducing the problem of finding a 2-edge-coloring for G, by identifying a minimal subset of edges with inconsistent degree discrepancies in G. If such a subset is not found, then we claim that G, a graph with a specific degree k, has the property of being 2-edge-colorable. We achieve this by making two main claims, both of which involve proving that a graph with a specific degree k, has the property of being 2-edge-colorable.
