The relationships between weighted Bergman spaces in the unit disk are studied, specifically focusing on how these spaces relate to $L^p$ from 0 to infinity based on the growth properties and integrability conditions of the functions involved.

This study introduces a versatile computer vision model capable of detecting COVID
and other respiratory infections by analyzing retaken chest X-ray images.
Initially, the model processes standard frontal CXR images with its primary
feature extraction module, comprising a UNET-like architecture. To enhance its
diagnostic capabilities, we incorporate retaken CXR images taken after deep
inspiration breaths. The model's implementation is available on GitHub at
https://github.com/alexamor/COVID_RI.

Our research demonstrates that incorporating clinical data improves the model's
sensitivity and accuracy. The results also indicate that using retaken CXR images
significantly enhance the model's performance, both in terms of its accuracy and
clinical usefulness. The model achieved an accuracy of 93.66% when using standard
images, but only used retaken images from patients who, according to clinical
notes, had pneumonia. The model's high sensitivity and accuracy make it an
excellent option for applications where recall is more critical than precision.

This research focuses on reducing the large and sparse distributions of low-earth orbit (LEO) satellites created by mega-constellations. We introduce minimum space occupancy (MiSO) orbits - patterns in three-dimensional space that allow satellites to stay within a specified distance of each other while maintaining the minimum amount of spatial overlap. Based on this concept, our goal is to design a network of non-interactive, stationary Levi robots, each carrying a single satellite, located within a specified radius from each other. We define a collision with another robot as occurring when the distance between them is less than or equal to 1, and our objective is to find a constant-scale solution for robot placement that minimizes the number of collisions and keeps Levi robots stationary. This is achieved through analyzing the mathematical properties of the problem and leveraging a recent result to show that a solution exists at a specific scale, and that it places satellites in specific spacings and heights to minimize spacinal overlap. We define a collision with a non-MiSO configuration as occurring when two or more robots within a specified radius form the same pattern, and our objective is to find a constant-scale solution for robot placement that minimizes the number of these collisions as well. We show that this solution exists at a specific scale, and that it places satellites in specific spacings and heights to minimize spatial overlap with other Levi robots. Furthermore, our method achieves a constant-factor approximation for robot placement that minimizes the number of Levi robots required to achieve this configuration

In an effort to speed up mesh generation, we propose a novel, quick method for generating quadrilateral meshes based on existing Delaunay triangulations. Although straightforward, this approach involves resolving certain conflicts by resplitting some elements. Importantly, this process simplifies the typically complicated and time-consuming refinement of quad layouts. Furthermore, a constructed T-mesh laid out according to an efficient, O(n log n) schema supports seamless integration with a wide range of mesh generation schemes, such as boundary-point-based or snappy mesh generation, via this simple advanced method.

When using the linear regression model to evaluate the correlation between variables x and y based on a sample of data, it's typical to assess the significance of the correlation coefficient by comparing p-values derived from various null hypotheses, with the underlying data distribution often assumed to be normal. However, when the actual distribution of the data deviates from this assumption, p-values may become unreliable, leading to an increase in Type I errors. This study proposes a new method for estimating p-values without prior knowledge of the data's underlying distribution. It uses a non-parametric density model based on nearest neighbors to estimate the sampling distribution of the usual correlation estimator, allowing the method to be applied to datasets with any probability distribution. The proposed approach is evaluated through simulation experiments, comparing its performance with other competing methods. The results show that this method performs well in certain data scenarios and offers a promising alternative for datasets with non-normal distributions. It's also shown that a variant of this method can be used to estimate the parameter of a heteroscedastic parametric model and that its asymptotic efficiency increases when the model's parameter is known. As an example of this method's utility, it's used to investigate the correlation between soybean yields and temperature in a real-world dataset.

A theoretical method known as the quantum $S$-matrix plays a crucial role in research regarding the quantum gravitational sector. This paper adapts the $S$-matrix formalism specifically for the context of static black hole metrics. We focus on the Schwarzschild and Reissner-Nordstrom black holes for our initial examination, followed by the analysis of the extrema of the black holes, namely, the Cauchy horizon and the event horizon. We then apply the $S$-matrix approach to calculate a black hole $S$-matrix parameterized by various key factors, including the in/out masses and the chemical potentials for the Reissner-Nordstrom case. We also identify a specific relationship regarding the mass parameter, which serves as an challenge to the conventional model of space-time.

We investigate the local stabilization properties of the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equation when controlled at specific points in space, specifically when the equation operates near an unstable equilibrium with chaotic dynamics. It has been shown that using these localized controls can sometimes yield exponential stabilization, but this is dependent on the controls' specific properties and locations. Essentially, we establish a set of conditions under which the time it takes for the solution to settle down after the controls are applied decreases exponentially with the distance to the unstable equilibrium. Notably, we prove that in the range of unstable dynamics, only spatially localized feedback that includes energy dissipation everywhere in the domain can prevent the occurrence of large-scale vortices. This result has implications for developing efficient and numerically stable algorithms using artificial gravity sources to orient artificial swimmers.

The LitMind Dictionary is an English-French dictionary that offers automated translation and definition generation for over 40 languages, including those spoken in India and Southeast Asia. To provide accurate results, the dictionary relies on a neural network that directly processes word inputs and avoids typical translation errors. However, the dictionary's reliance on this architecture also means it is susceptible to the fake word phenomenon, where fake words are incorrectly translated due to minor changes in the word's spelling. To combat this issue, we have developed a fake word filter based on a specially trained model designed to identify real words. Our model, developed using the WikiText-103 language model, is the first effective filter developed using an external language model, as proven by tests conducted on several fake word datasets.

A growing number of recommender systems are being designed with explainability in mind, using methods like tree ensembles and neural networks to elicit interpretations of their decision-making processes. Despite these efforts, it's noteworthy that research has yet to thoroughly assess the reliability of the insights these models offer. We investigate the effect of post-hoc explanation methods on recomender systems and discover that a critical issue arises with the post-hoc explanations provided by these models. A large majority of post-hoc explanation methods generate explanations using training data, which may not accurately represent test data, thereby limiting the utility of the explanations. Using recoder attacks on several recommendation models and datasets, we successfully deceived all the models into producing misleading explanations over 90% of the time. We extend the test to focus on a subset of the explanations, namely, the top-rated item explanations, for a larger group of models. Moreover, we find strong evidence supporting the notion that recommender systems are Robustness-Explanation Inconsistent (RII), and this inconsistency holds true across various explanation techniques and datasets. Furthermore, we develop a novel metric, called Explanation Certificates (E-Cert), which provides sufficient certificates to identify the true items that a model ranks higher than others, and this metric turns out to be significantly weaker than what the current explanation methods can produce. Based on our findings, we provide recommendations for future research directions.

Research on the electronic properties of the surface states of InAs(111) and its hybrid metal, GaAs(111), has been conducted using high-resolution photoemission spectroscopy, with and without applied voltage. Our findings reveal that a thin In$_{0.81}$Al$_{0.19}$As capping layer eliminates the excess charge on the surface of InAs, whereas the same capping layer charged when it comes to GaAs. Moreover, the natural surface states on GaAs(111) are not sufficiently energetic to be detected within measurement range. In InAs/In$_{0.81}$Al$_{0.19}$As, the introduction of a thin In$_{0.81}$Al$_{0.19}$As capping layer brings the surface electronic density close to neutrality, with no visible spillover charge from the 2D InAs electron gas. Our measurements reveal that the interface electron charge is much smaller than that of a single InAs surface, and also that the hybrid metal surface has minimal interaction with its covalent metal counterpart. Our data also indicate that the excess charge on the InAs surface is significantly reduced, whereas the hybrid metal surface has minimal reduction in excess charge. Our findings are in agreement with the theoretical prediction that the excess charge on the InAs surface is mainly due to the electronic charge from the spillover 2D InAs electron gas, and that the hybrid metal surface has minimal reduction in excess

In a Euclidean space of dimension n, we examine robust concept classes defined on queries within a radius r, which have a condition that involves the ratio of the concept class's diameter to the query radius, denoted as D(r), less than or equal to 1/n. For empirical risk minimization processes, our analysis shows that when n is much larger than the logarithm of the sample size, and given a certain level of perturbation via noiser with relative dimension roughly 1/n, these processes achieve robust robustness at a rate comparable to optimal least-squared error rates, which validates a long-standing assumption in robust machine learning. Specifically, our results cover cases for quadratic and convolutional neural networks, which are trained with least-squared loss under certain conditions. Additionally, we established robust robustness for random feature models and kernel ridge regression with robust generalization by applying a distributionally robust via Lagrangian relaxation, which involves the Kullback-Liebler distance, and showed that when the noiser dimension is much larger than the query radius, it results in computationally viable solutions with Lagrangian relaxation having an upper bound that is polynomial in n.

The FS-2 algorithm, a variation of the Sinkhorn algorithm, enhances the efficiency of computing optimal transport through the use of a unique loss function that is computed in line with the Sinkhorn iterations, unlike its pointwise counterparts. This algorithm's superiority is demonstrated in terms of computational efficiency and memory usage. While maintaining a similar number of iterations as Sinkhorn, FS-2 scales much better in terms of memory usage and losses, particularly beneficial for large datasets. Moreover, FS-2's simplicity enables real-time performance, even on a simple GPU, making it a practical solution for large-scale computations.

The existence of the young exoplanet AU Mic b remains mysterious due to its proximity to its host star. A recent study observed atmospheric fluctuations in the planet's reflected light and sought to understand the planet's mass-loss patterns by analyzing these changes, assuming that the variations were caused by the interactions between the planet's atmosphere and its stellar environment. Three distinct patterns of atmospheric loss were discovered, each corresponding to different phases of the host star's activity levels. The primary method to understand these loss patterns relied on analyzing the changes in the planet's reflection light and mapping them onto a graph, known as an EW-EW diagram. When the host star's activity levels surge during flares, the planet's mass-loss rate increases dramatically from $3.4\ times 10^{-13}$ to $1.1\ times 10^{-12}$ times the mass of the sun per year. In contrast, when the host star's activity levels are relatively low, this rate decreases to $1.1\ times 10^{-14}$ to $3.4\ times 10^{-14}$ times the mass of the sun per year. Additionally, when the host star's activity levels are moderate, this rate increases to $8.4\ times 10^{-14}$ to $2.5\ times 10^{-13}$ times the mass of the sun per year. Investigating electron dynamics within a turbulent plasma gas that is also experiencing radiation pressure, we discover a generalized form of this phenomenon. This investigation expands on the concept of "matter-induced radiation friction" and reveals how a particle's movement causes strain in the medium, which in turn affects the radiation pressure and particle dynamics in a cyclic pattern. Consequently, we derived an extended, modified Lorentz force equation that takes into account both classical and quantum friction effects. Furthermore, we have developed a novel, two-way coupling model that links particle and medium interactions through collective radiation fields, which provides fresh insights into the distribution and behavior of hot, flowing plasma electrons. We have also explored the potential novel applications of this theoretical model in understanding both ultra-high-energy, relativistic and quantum-scale particle dynamics.

This research introduces three novel ensemble-based approaches to tackle the challenge of imbalanced data. These classifiers create synthetic examples within the underrepresented class of data, aiming to boost minority class prediction accuracy. In contrast to existing oversampling techniques that modify the class distribution, our methods involve creating a new synthetic majority class based on the original distribution. Our approach builds upon the current best practice, pre-processing techniques used in oversampling, and assesses the effectiveness of our novel distribution maintenance methods across 10 imbalanced datasets. Our experimental findings suggest that our novel methods surpass the existing methods in accuracy for the minority class, while exhibiting comparable or improved f-measure, precision, recall rates, and overall classification accuracy. Our distribution maintenance methods outperform the current state-of-the-art methods due to their ability to enhance minority class prediction accuracy without negatively impacting the majority class. Our novel approaches ensure that the synthetic examples created maintain a balanced distribution, differentiating them from existing oversampling techniques.

Twenty high-redshift Quasi-Stellar Objects (QSOs) have been discovered in the southern hemisphere as part of the Wide-Field QSO Survey II (WQSS2), which was conducted using four plates from the AAOePODS program matched to archival ESO images. The newly found QSOs have absolute magnitudes more than two times greater than the survey's limit and were detected between 2000 < z < 5.7 with a success rate of over 99%. The discoveries were made at a rate of approximately 4250 square degrees, confirming that the survey will find over 100 new QSOs above z=5.7 within a 7000 square degree area. The QSOs were primarily found at redshifts between 5.7 and 5.9, highlighting the significance of finding these rare objects. The interplay between a quantum dot and a superconductor offers a unique platform to explore the superconductor's energy gap through quantum measurement. By treating the quantum dot as a sensing device within a three-terminal setup, where the superconductor's lead is isolated from the lead that drives the quantum dot, we derive an explicit expression for the quantum dot's current-voltage characteristics. Under these specific conditions, the quantum dot functions as a detector to identify the specific energy levels within the superconductor's energy gap. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the quantum dot's conductance acts as a probe to determine the width of the superconductor's energy gap. Our theoretical findings align precisely with experimental data obtained from a study conducted by Ferrus et al., which investigates the interplay between a InAs quantum dot and Al superconductor using tunneling spectroscopy. Our results suggest that the superconductor's energy gap is not perfectly symmetric and that its width in the lower branch measures approximately 0.48 meV, roughly half of 0.96 meV found in the upper branch.

This research focuses on the analytical analysis of a specific type of shock solution in magnetohydrodynamic fluids with two dimensions and enthalpy. The study discovers that intermediate shocks have a contraction property and finds that principal symbols of hyperbolic operators associated with an extended Kornowodt problem have distinct properties in the type of shock they represent. The study also discovers that waves generated by an S-kink have a unique property of being able to intersect at a specific point without meeting halfway, which is not found in the analysis of simple shocks. The study also leverages this analysis to demonstrate that hyperbolic operator symbols play a crucial role in the determination of shock speeds and shows that when the magnetic field ratio meets a specific condition, shocks become nonlinear and develop at a specific point, with the type of shock being an example of a more complex type of shock. The study also touches on the relationship between intermediate shocks and other types of shock solutions in this system.

This research explores the challenge of perpetual view generation in computer vision, a task that demands an endless sequence of novel images around a fixed viewpoint, and is pivotal in several vision applications including panoramic mosaics, 3D modeling, and robotic mapping. Existing methods for panoramic image creation have fallen short, necessitating numerous reconstructions over time to generate high-quality images. In contrast, our proposed Deep Image Composite (DIC) method allows for the composite creation of a high-quality image stream using just one pass and no prior knowledge, and is based on a simplified image formation model that positions cameras based on look-at positions and orientation. By mapping input images to a global, non-textured 3D mesh, and combining camera inputs at arbitrary viewpoints, DIC achieves seamless image fusion without artifacts. Our experiments demonstrate that DIC outperforms previous techniques, producing superior results in panoramic mosaics, feature-based image synthesis, and 3D reconstruction, and validating our new image composite algorithm.

In large-scale complex networks, real-time control through optimization methods faces significant computational challenges. To tackle this issue and speed up computational processing, researchers are exploring the application of the Koopman operator to model predictive control techniques. This paper presents a novel approach that utilizes the spectral properties of linear systems represented by the Koopman operator to model and improve computational efficiency of temporal dynamics in complex networks. This method converts nonlinear dynamics into linear equations using the Koopman operator, offering a more efficient approach for model predictive control. Importantly, our results indicate that the spectral properties of the Koopman operator in time-delay systems can be easily obtained without regard to system size or number of time delays, thus facilitating the rapid modeling of large-scale complex time-delay systems. This paper demonstrates the practical application of the Koopman operator in finite-time optimal control of time-delay systems with constraints, employing the finite-horizon optimal solution derived using the Koopman operator to yield quick and accurate solutions even for large-scale systems. Our numerical studies confirm that the application of the Koopman operator results in significantly reduced computational time, up to thousands of times faster, to solve optimal control problems in time-delay systems.

A fibre with a liquid film attaching it to a plane is examined, where a film droplet forms at the fibre's base due to a specific slip condition applied transversely to the fibre's axis. In this instance, analytical solutions derived from a model developed by de Gennes, which involves a semi-infinite fibre, accurately represent the droplet's shape and the fibre's detachment point. Notably, the model exhibits a novel transition, where the fibre's detachment point changes from a constant to a varying value, depending on the fibre's length and detachment location. This transition occurs when a specific non-dimensional parameter, influenced by the fibre's slip condition and a balance between surface tension and van der Waals forces, crosses a critical threshold. In contrast to fibre models with a fibre-driven slip condition, this transition is attributed primarily to the detachment mechanism rather than adhesion. Additionally, a model considering both fibre and attachment points moving over time shows that as the fibre's slip condition becomes more extended, the fibre's detachment point increases with time, while at critical and wetting cases, the fibre's detachment point reaches a constant value.

The Lagrangian description of fluid dynamics involves local parameters such as fluid element velocity and deformation rate, distinguishing it from the Eulerian description based on spatial metrics. In the Lagrangian framework, physical laws are typically applied at the level of individual fluid elements, whose motion complies with the standard continuum mechanics model when no external forces are present. We prove that if no external forces act on fluid elements in Lagrangian space, those elements follow the straightforward equation ${\mathbf F} \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0$, where ${\mathbf F}$ represents the deformation gradient tensor. Surprisingly, this simple condition is sufficient to ensure that Eulerian space metrics coincide with their Lagrangian counterparts when no external forces are present. We further illustrate that consistent metrics can be assigned to a passive element flowing through a general $N$-manifold without external forces being applied.

To determine the accuracy of robotic ultrasound in measuring the angles of spinal vertebrae using artificial intelligence, we compared the results with data from X-ray scans, considering both within-patient and between-patient variability. Six scoliosis patients underwent both ultrasound and X-ray imaging on the same day, with the robotic ultrasound featuring automatic alignment with each vertebra. The study's focus was on the evaluation of the robotic ultrasound's reliability in estimating the angles of spinal vertebrae using the within-patient approach, as well as the accuracy of its measurements in comparing the obtained angles with those from X-ray scans. The results showed that the robotic ultrasound produced relatively accurate measurements of the angles of spinal vertebrae, with within-patient reliability coefficients ranging between 0.80 and 0.90 for the calculation of vertebral angles and 0.70 to 0.90 for fusion angles. The study's findings therefore indicate that the use of robotic ultrasound may be a reliable and accurate method for monitoring the progression of scoliosis, including the estimation of spinal curvature using computer-based imaging technology. Future studies are, however, needed to further validate the results.

We introduce a novel temporal model called TempORe for temporal reasoning in reasoning on temporal information in machine reading comprehension tasks. Unlike traditional Duration Network models, which rely on continuous duration distributions, TempORe uses discrete duration levels and models their implications. The network comprises two components: a Temporal Unit Converter that translates temporal intervals to uniform durations, and a temporal reader that extracts task-specific temporal insights, combining these with temporal unit conversions to yield precise readings. The model's general applicability is demonstrated through experiments on task-specific temporal understanding scenarios. Further research could explore extending TempORe to tackle complex temporal reasoning challenges across multiple domains.

We've conducted a study to explore the application of Transfer Learning with BERT in detecting hateful content within South Asian communities, employing a dataset of semi-annotated posts gathered from social media, encompassing Hindi, Urdu, and Bengali languages. By comparing various NLP approaches and models, our investigation revealed that BERT, when fine-tuned with a convolutional model, yielded the most successful results. We've also highlighted several linguistic patterns observed in our data, suggesting further research is needed to develop more effective hateful content detection that leverages NLP, is language-agnostic, and tailored to diverse online communities.

A recent study suggested using multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) autoencoders for dimensionality reduction in biomedical data. However, biomedical datasets exhibit inherent complexities due to various data subgroups, causing standard MIMO autoencoders to lose critical subgroup distinctions during the compression process. This work aims to mitigate this limitation by introducing a novel step – explicit subgroup unmixing – incorporated within a MIMO framework. The proposed framework comprises two primary components: an feature extraction step utilizing MIMO autoencoders to minimize the data dimension, and subsequent accurate subgroup unmixing from the compressed data. Various numerical simulations have been conducted to evaluate the proposed framework's effectiveness, using MIMO with deep convolutional neural networks. Furthermore, the proposed framework has been successfully applied to multi-energy single photon counting camera compressed data, effectively retrieving the original subgroup information from the compressed data and demonstrating substantial accuracy improvements in high-energy spectral estimation compared to other techniques.

Historical document analysis encompasses a diverse range of research activities that involve the computational processing of documents from the past. These documents can take the form of printed materials such as books, articles, and photographs, or digital content like email archives and social media updates. One of the primary challenges in this field is identifying and selecting relevant datasets, as existing collections often exclude significant areas of study due to their limited scope and focus on specific, sometimes obscure topics. This research draws on the principles of software engineering to develop a dataset selection framework grounded in object-oriented design, with the goal of addressing this challenge and facilitating more efficient access to existing datasets. By exploiting the benefits of inheritance and polymorphism, our system enables the creation of a versatile dataset choice mechanism that is well-suited to addressing diverse research needs. Although the focus of this work is on contributing a novel approach to the field, the accompanying implementation serves as a valuable resource, providing a versatile tool for researchers to engage in historical document analysis.

This research offers a compliance-based approach to enhancing the accuracy of linear trajectory tracking for industrial robots. This method converts nonlinear current commands into precise angular positions via a displacement amplifier, ensuring that the end-effector follows a trajectory with the same dynamics as a rigid joint. Unlike traditional approaches, our compliance-based solution accounts for all joint actuators when calculating the required end-effector displacement. This method's effectiveness was evaluated using a KUKA Nova 180 4+ six-axis robotic arm during experiments involving various joints. These experiments compared the motion of a compliant end-effector with that of a traditional one, achieving significant improvements in trajectory tracking accuracy. Specifically, our compliance-based approach reduced position errors by 1.9-2.6 mm, 0.8-1.2 mm, and 0.6-1.0 mm in the X, Y, and Z axes, respectively. These gains were achieved along with reduced velocity errors of 0.2-0.3 m/s, 0.1 m/s, and 0.1 m/s in the X, Y, and Z axes, respectively.

Myocardial infarction survivors who experience a second event are disproportionately affected by multiple long-term health conditions.
The awareness of this issue in the UK healthcare system motivates research that involves:
  a) Identifying patients who have experienced two or more myocardial infarctions and analysing the patterns of their co-occurring health conditions.
  b) Comparing the results with data from patients who have only had one myocardial infarction to highlight any significant discrepancies.
  c) Investigating socio-demographic variations in the patterns of these co-occurring health conditions.
  d) Using eHealth records and eHealth records with informed consent to inform the development of healthcare systems that predict and prevent myocardial infarctions.
  e) Developing a healthcare system that facilitates early intervention and reduces the likelihood of a second myocardial infarction.

The research found that patients with two or more myocardial infarctions have a unique set of co-occurring health conditions that differ from those of patients with only one myocardial infinction.
The study showed that there are significant socio-demographic variations in the patterns of health conditions, particularly with regard to sex and ethnicity, as well as age.
The researchers used visualisations to facilitate understanding of the data and opened the door for future research in this area to further refine the knowledge gained.

Regarding the development of a healthcare system, the researchers pointed out potential issues with data sharing and highlighted the necessity of creating a secure data-sharing platform.

We introduce a revised version of Becke's scheme for handling divergent terms associated with the electronic continuum, enabling more efficient convergence of critical integrals in relativistic methods. Unlike non-relativistic implementations that rely on a global threshold for discontinuous functions, our revised approach incorporates a spatially dependent criterion tied to the finite-range function's value, which efficiently converges integrals to within numerical precision. Furthermore, our revised scheme retains the global continuity of relativistic correlation energies, while substantially improving convergence rates for the explicit value of the discontinuity term. We assess the performance of these merged relativistic correlation energy formulas using benchmark data for small diatomic molecules.

The Metric Dimension parameterized by vertex cover receives a thorough analysis, demonstrating that it belongs to the W[1] class and is hard within this class to be fixed-parameter tractable. Conversely, we find Metric Dimension parameterized by vertex cover to be fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the genus of the graph, and similarly when parameterized by the tree width. This contrast highlights the significance of the choice of parameterization for understanding the complexity of problem Metric Dimension.

In contrast to spaces with partial orders and Scott topology, directed spaces' upper, lower, and convex space representations cannot be reduced to their respective ordered counterparts. We provide an outline of the construction in a separate document.

In "Climate of the Past" journal, our research delves into how warm regional climates in the past relied heavily on water. By using a state-of-the-art computer model to analyze these climates, we discovered that warm climates used water to regulate their temperature, which led to increased humidity levels, more frequent clouds and greater precipitation. This past model is unique as it naturally regulates its temperature without using external adjustments and relies on the same atmospheric processes as the current models. This research is part of a larger project that aims to improve the accuracy of current climate models by validating them against historical climate data.

We examine the higher-spin expansion of Yang-Mills theory, focusing on its free quark sector and finding that the rescaled fields of the full theory match those of an unfolded theory for the top component. However, an analogy with the fundamental vector field of Yang-Mills theory reveals that the rescaled fields of the full theory do not form a fundamental field. Instead, the rescaled fields can be reinterpreted as a fundamental vector field with non-trivial symmetries such as double copy relationships. Additionally, the higher-spin action for Yang-Mills theory offers a flat section structure that naturally leads to Dirac and Majorana spinors with an unfolded action that matches Witten's proposal.

Deep learning networks have effectively solved a range of issues in the fields of speech and remote sensing, but they are susceptible to suboptimal performance when encountering noisy data. To counter this, a new Bayesian statistics-based method called BLRM is proposed, which not only recovers the accurate labels but also enhances the efficiency of the training process. BLRM's effectiveness is demonstrated through its implementation in a new statistical model called the variable interval hidden Markov model (VHMM), a type of deep neural network (DNN) that uses BLRM for both supervision and training. The results from the speech and remote sensing datasets show that BLRM can recover labels precision of 99%, while the BLRM-guided VHMM model exhibits improved robustness in noisy environments, reduced training error rate (TER), and higher HQR accuracy compared to the traditional supervised VHMM, even in the presence of low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs).

A problem originally posed by Roth is addressed, concerning the existence of a non-degenerate regular simplex within the unit cube $\Q_n$ in $\R^n$ with vertices defined by the intersection of the principal hyperplanes. In the event that $\R^n$ is equipped with the $l_\infty$ norm, Roth demonstrated the existence of such a non-degenerate simplex under the condition that $n \geq 2h + 3$ and $h$ is an integer. However, an analysis by Garling revealed that $n \geq 2h + 2$ would be the minimum required for the presence of a non-degenerate, regular $k$-simplex in $\Q_n$. Nonetheless, despite extensive research spanning over fifty years, the problem of determining whether $\R^n$ allows for the existence of non-degenerate, regular simplices in $\Q_n$ under the $l_\infty$ norm with an equal distance of intersection remains an open one. In the present study, it is shown that for $n \geq 4$ and $l=n$, $\R^n$ does not admit a non-degenerate, regular simplex with an equal distance of intersection in $\Q_n$. Furthermore, it is found that for $n \geq 5$, $\R^n$ does not support the existence of a non-degenerate, regular simplex with an equal distance of intersection in $\Q_n$ even when the norm is Euclidean

We analyze a class of correlated random walks within a finite state space, 
characterized by a countably infinite transition probability matrix, 
displaying periodic behavior on average, as evidenced by the non-zero determinant 
of the transition probability matrix's generating function. A specific sub-class is identified 
with a distinct transition probability matrix structure, facilitating a direct computation 
of the transition probability matrix's characteristic polynomial as a polynomial 
multiplication of integer values. Additionally, an inverse laplace transform approach 
is taken to derive an asymptotic formula for the longest subsequence of non-periodic states.

Proving the termination of complex functions is a challenging task in programming, often requiring a thorough understanding of the functions' inner workings. In this study, we outline a new approach to simplifying such proofs by restructuring the functions to minimize the use of a clock variable in their definitions, which are then examined through the lenses of co-inductive clock analysis and functional analysis. We have created a semi-algorithmic method for determining when a clock can be eliminated without further analysis, which we have coupled with a more in-depth, analytical method that provides guarantees. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique by illustrating its application to a variety of real-world programming examples, including the computation of graphs' transitive closures and the execution of logic programs with termination issues.

In descriptions of wall-bounded turbulence, the hairpin packet has been utilized, comprising a central hairpin vortex paired with an anti-parallel packet symmetric about the central branch. Previous studies suggested that the packet's components interact through a dynamic influence exerted by the central branch on the spiraling streamers positioned outside. This interaction has been found to transfer momentum and thereby connect the large-scale structure of the turbulent flow. This paper aims to offer an alternative, more refined explanation for the packet's dynamics by introducing an evolving structure, the rolling packet. A key aspect is that the packet's dynamics are neutral to translations along the spines and to rotations about them, allowing for a more accurate modeling of the hairpin packet's movement and growth. This refined explanation is then utilized to derive a mathematical equation describing the cumulative distribution of hairpin packets in turbulent flows, applied to wakes and airfoil cascades.

A gauged version of the baby Skyrme model is investigated. This model is based on a three-dimensional sphere space. It has been demonstrated that the Dyonic solitons, with electric and magnetic charges, are present in this model. The solitons exhibit three distinct profiles - skyrmion, hopfion, and taubion - whose stability is also examined. Notably, the taubion profile displays stability via the semi-dual bare tree level approach.

We investigate a lattice simulation of a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model incorporating both chiral and mirror symmetries within a lattice structure that combines non-orthogonal cells with mirror inversion symmetry. The phase diagram of this model is examined, revealing that in the presence of certain symmetries, the chiral liquid phase is protected, whereas other phases are susceptible to order-disorder transitions. The results of a high-order perturbation theory expound on the mechanisms driving the transitions and explore the effects of fluctuations. Additionally, the scenario where the above simulations include an additional time reversal symmetry is examined, demonstrating the emergence of a topological superconductor exhibiting quantized Josephson effects and a $\pi$-junction nature.

A novel nanoantenna design concept is introduced, which is capable of independently modulating its resonant frequencies. By combining a silicon membrane with a gold nanostructure and pairing it with an air gap, nanoantenna properties can be tailored to effectively interact with both surface and volume electromagnetic effects. Using nanoantennas of specifically designed shapes and placed in certain air-gap widths, researchers discovered the ability to modulate multiple light frequencies simultaneously with a single device. The interaction with the air gap influences a notable shift in the light spectrum, allowing for the customization of a silicon membrane-based nanoantenna's resonance properties. Additionally, incorporating a second metal layer enables the adjustment of a complementary nanoantenna's resonance frequencies, contributing to enhanced light control. This innovative design opens avenues for the effective modulation of light transmission among complementary nanoantennas and can serve as a foundation for developing efficient light sources and high-performance photodetectors.

Amorphous materials have long been overlooked due to their lack of microscopic order, but instead, they've developed a unique set of plastic events that significantly impact their mechanical properties. Studies have consistently shown how the plastic behavior of these materials differs from that of crystalline solids, with implications that can be explored beyond traditional mechanical properties. Our research investigates plastic events in a range of amorphous systems, including sand, glass, and biological tissue, using the framework of a mesoscale model that simulates a solid undergoing deformation. Our model operates within a universal framework that can be applied to a wide array of materials, which we've demonstrated by applying it to two seemingly disparate systems: amorphous biological tissue and sand. Our research confirms that the behavior of these systems, despite their differences in composition and as-yet-unknown structural details, exhibits striking similarities. Furthermore, we've seen evidence of plastic events in sand and being investigated as a potential mechanism governing biofluid behavior. Our findings underscore the importance of a universal approach to understanding and studying plasticity across different materials, from biological to geological systems.

The Hubbard model, a fundamental framework for studying electron interactions, has been applied to silicene with manganese decorations. Silicene, a narrow band material, exhibits significant electron correlations. Studies have focused on two different substitution sites for manganese within the two-orbital, two-sublattice Hubbard model: the top-site and the hollow-site configurations. For the former, a significant increase was observed in the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter when comparing decorated silicene to pristine silicene. In contrast, the Hubbard model's results for the hollow-site decoration revealed a contrasting trend. These findings are viewed through the lens of a mean-field theory, which identifies Fermi-sea hole hopping as the primary driver of increased Hubbard interactions. Additionally, calculations of the momentum-dependent exchange interaction highlight its significance in influencing electron correlations in manganese-decorated silicene.

The centre of the Milky Way harbours a compact radio and X-ray-emitting region known as Sgr A East. This area is surrounded by shell-like structures, believed to be the remnants of a supernova that exploded around 13--30 parsecs from the galaxy's centre. To understand Sgr A East's formation and development, researchers have been studying its surroundings using data from the Spitzer Space Telescope's mid-infrared wavelength range. In a 15 square degree area around the galaxy's centre, researchers searched for molecular structures containing oxygen-bearing species, including oxygen, water, and monoxide. They found a significant molecular structure, spanning approximately 100 parsecs in diameter and extending from the galaxy's centre towards the north-east, featuring molecular ratios similar to those of other similar structures in the galaxy. The structure, named OVI, is a column density of 10^20, features a significant change in density from 25 to 100 parsecs in diameter, and has an estimated average density of 10^17. The structure is believed to be part of a larger molecular disk extending from the galaxy's center towards the galaxy's bulge, and is oriented in the direction of the galaxy's central supermassive black hole.

This paper investigates the effect of oversampling, undersampling, and the Allometry technique on various machine learning algorithms, including KNN, SVM, and neural networks, in dealing with class imbalance. Our experiments show that oversampling and undersampling methods yield better outcomes for KNN and SVM but the Allometry method surpasses these methods in performance. Interestingly, oversampling and undersampling methods do not outperform the Allometry method for neural networks. Notably, neural networks exhibit significantly less impact from class imbalance compared to KNN and SVM, showing a slight decrease or no difference in performance on imbalanced data. Our findings suggest that KNN and SVM generally benefit from using Allometry, whereas neural networks can already achieve similar results without it. Moreover, a simple post-processing technique based on the Allometry method can improve the performance of neural networks on imbalanced data. Our code is available online at https://github.com/KarlovicFilip/Madars-Oversampling.git.

The COVID-19 pandemic led to a sharp decline in national advertising, forcing many small and local newspapers in the United States to temporarily shut down due to limited revenue. In this study, we analyzed the economic and news output impacts of this crisis, focusing on 47,040 daily and weekly newspapers across the US. First, we used data from Google Analytics to understand COVID-related search volume variations and how they related to news consumption across different regions. Next, we utilized Google News Aggregator data to measure the volume and content of local news coverage regarding COVID-19, as well as the overall circulation of newspapers. In addition, we merged Advox's news volume data with revenue information from the Pew Research Center to determine the correlation between circulation and news output. Our results showed that regional COVID incidence, working age population, and news consumption significantly influenced both the volume and content of local news coverage. However, we found no significant link between COVID incidence and news output. Moreover, we discovered a limited effect of national COVID incidence on news output, whereas a stronger connection was present for working age population. These factors ultimately contributed to varying levels of local news coverage. During the pandemic, communities with higher COVID rates, working age population, or limited news consumption tended to have reduced news volume.

A new N-body implementation within the open-source code, PEnGuIN, utilizes the Fast Multipole Method to accelerate the computation of pairwise interactions between particles, especially for astrophysical time-evolution simulations requiring a large number of high-precision time steps. This FMM-enabled N-body algorithm is now the default implementation in PEnGuIN and is the primary method discussed in this study, though the code also includes an alternative O(N) Newton-CG method for situations requiring even higher speed. By adapting the publicly available HiFiLib library, PEnGuIN's N-body code incorporates a FMM algorithm optimized for floating point triple precision arithmetic, a first in the context of Fast Multipole Method-based algorithms. To ensure the accuracy of FMM computations, a comprehensive analysis of errors is performed and a precision-adaptive time-stepping scheme is implemented that accounts for potential errors in force and energy calculations while maintaining a user-specified level of energy uncertainty. This scheme allows for a dynamic trade-off between computational speed and numerical accuracy, making it suitable for a range of astrophysical simulations requiring precision estimates. To validate the implementation, a series of tests involving homogeneous, radially symmetric, and Gaussian distributions were conducted, evaluating the accuracy and performance of the N-body algorithm. These experiments demonstrated a >20x speed-up compared to a standard, Lennard-Jones based, N-body algorithm while still enabling precise control over energy uncertainty to <10^-6 in certain cases. We have analyzed the $e^{-} e^{+} p p$ process for $J/\psi$ and $\Upsilon$ production at an $e^{-} e^{+} \text{GeV}$ collider, focusing on a specific measurement - the double spin asymmetry $\alpha_J$, which indicates in $J/\psi$ and $\Upsilon$ production, both particle and antiparticle contribute to the initial helion state. The value of $\alpha_J$ for $J/\psi$ at $s=4.2$ GeV is found to be $0.8 \pm 0.3$ (statistical) $^{+0.0}$ (-systematic) $^{+0.1}$ (syntactic) error. If the $\Upsilon$ result equals $J/\psi$, it would be a proof that $\alpha_J$ does not rely on the $c$ or $b$ quark mass. Furthermore, we consider $\phi$ production and determine the double spin asymmetry $\alpha_\phi$ to be $0.9 \pm 0.3$ (stat.) $^{+0.0}$ (-systematic) $^{+0.1}$ (synt.) error at $s=4.2$ GeV.

Deep reinforcement learning has faced challenges in transferring skilled behavior from expert to student agents, particularly in control problems with numerous dimensions of control. This research focuses on "policy cloning" - a technique where the teacher's control policy is mimicked without performance feedback or guidance. While previous studies demonstrated policy cloning's potential in low-dimensional control, this work adapts the approach for high-dimensional control by presenting a new method. This novel technique bridges the gap between demonstration and execution by leveraging a detailed, explicit model of the teacher's control actions and utilizes a generative adversarial network to discover the teacher's latent representation. Moreover, the student learns to replicate the teacher's latent representation and discovers its underlying factors, enabling them to generalize and adapt when working with incomplete or changing demonstration data. This study's results on two complex robotic tasks - a 21D direct joint control problem and a 122D positional control problem - demonstrate the successful application of policy cloning in high-dimensional control.

A recent study investigated the production of Higgs bosons via high-energy collisions at the LHC, specifically focusing on the role of space-time modulated Higgs bosons. This study considered the creation of a Higgs boson along with a top-quark pair, and accounted for the influence of background processes. Analyzing the Shsh and Shp channels for Higgs bosons with CP-zero and CP-1 states revealed observable signals for heavy scalar and pseudoscalar resonances with masses between 220 and 350 GeV and 260 and 320 GeV, respectively. Although the signals were weaker than those from the standard model's top-quark pair production processes, they were still expected to be detectable at the LHC. This study also projected the potential sensitivity of the future HL-LHC and FCC-hh facilities to reveal the existence of these new Higgs bosons.

Research on resonant spin masers, fueled by potential quantum technologies, has prompted an investigation into a novel two-stage resonant spin maser design incorporating digital signal processing. The outcome revealed that, contrary to initial expectations, digital signal processing did not yield improved performance but instead led to performance degradation. Furthermore, it was found that this new design did not exhibit the improved performance gains seen in conventional masers incorporating digital signal processing. The observed outcomes suggested that digital signal processing could be tailored to produce desirable outcomes by selectively modulating pump rate and resonance frequency. Building upon this insight, a two-stage resonant spin maser design incorporating digital signal processing was developed, resulting in the production of sidebands outside the main frequency range with diminished power, thus providing a means to fine-tune the system to detect hidden signals.

We've found an infinite number of hypergeometric groups, which we're calling H, and each can be linked to specific K3 surface automorphisms. Notably, H encompasses a broader range of K3 surface automorphisms compared to groups derived from iterative applications of the Nielsen-Thurston classification. Our research demonstrates that certain properties of the group, such as its rank and faithful actions, can be easily proven. Additionally, H's parent hypergeometric groups have more intricate Lie algebra representations compared to groups derived from the Nielsen-Thurston classification.

We propose a novel search strategy to detect neutralino decays into hidden matter through gamma-ray observations. In the visible sector, a neutralino decays into a hidden neutralino and a high-energy gamma, which may be absorbed by the Earth's magnetic field, resulting in an energetic gamma origin uncertainty. This leads to an increased geometric factor and enhanced sensitivity to the visible-to-hidden neutralino mass ratio. Our analysis, performed using the HESS dataset, fails to reveal a signal from the Galactic Center. This results in constraints on the visible and hidden neutralino mass ratios at 100 GeV, with ratios greater than approximately 10~100 GeV in the mass range of 1-100 GeV. Our future prospects indicate that the Cherenkov Observatories may achieve similar or lower gamma uncertainty and comparable sensitivity to the visible-to-hidden neutralino mass ratio ratios. Additionally, future experiments at particle colliders such as the LHC and CLIC are expected to explore complementary mass regions.

A fundamental question in graph theory asks for a precise definition of a graph's genus based on its minimal surface embedding. To address this, a graph's genus function is introduced, representing the set of all possible genus values for a given graph in ascending order. Furthermore, another function is considered, mapping a graph to the least possible genus of its simplest surface embedding. In a notable observation, certain graph families featuring high genus values include those with extremely high genus values. In a distinct example, a genus function was found to increase steadily with increasing graph size. In a notable advancement, a comprehensive and detailed classification of all possible genus functions was established for graphs consisting of up to six vertices. In a distinct example, a detailed investigation of a specific graph, consisting of six vertices and 21 edges, found that its genus function increases steadily with increasing graph size. In a distinct example, a specific graph function, consisting of five vertices and 10 edges, was found to increase steadily with increasing graph size. In a distinct example, a detailed investigation of a specific graph, consisting of five vertices and 10 edges, found that its genus value is equal to one. In stochastic optimization, the speed of solution processing can be improved by optimizing the speed of communication transfers, which is counterintuitive yet true. By mirroring local random sampling in a model problem and using it to modify a communication-impeded stochastic gradient descent, we achieve a method that mimics variance-reduced acceleration using efficient data transfer. The new approach retains a similar rate of solution processing as its optimal counterpart but now facilitates faster data transfer, which is substantiated by relevant experimental findings that supplement the theoretical results. Besides its inherent practicality, this processing technique has a broader implications in-concept simplicity makes it valuable as a building block in developing more faster and efficient solution processing methods.

Our study explores the potential for cross-lingual knowledge transfer in morphology
and syntax through transfer learning, particularly in languages with shared roots.
Focusing on two sets of languages with known genealogical connections, we extend
existing cross-lingual models to incorporate family-level relationships, effectively
expanding the linguistic scope without increasing model complexity. The results
demonstrate substantial enhancements in relative precision when leveraging genealogical
information, with notable gains in morphological transfer ranging from 44.8% to
67.2% and modest gains in syntactic transfer ranging from 10.3% to 18.9%. The
outcome suggests that incorporating genealogical information can significantly aid
model training in languages with shared ancestry. Furthermore, the excessive
capacity of deep cross-lingual models, which allows them to capture genetic
relationships, is highlighted as a limitation, underscoring the need for future
research to develop more targeted models that prioritize syntax over genealogy.

We propose and evaluate a set of new observables that can differentiate between electron and nuclear recoils in Gas Time Projection Chambers using recently simulated data from the DarkSide-50 experiment. This includes a reduced observable space that retains discrimination capabilities, allowing for lower light yields and smaller observables. We demonstrate the potential for these new observables to perform well in dark matter research in liquid argon detectors.

The value of driver behavior data collected from monitoring vehicles lies in its potential to optimize road network design and improve safety by providing objective insights into driving conditions. Nonetheless, the subjectivity involved in driver behavior assessment limits the usefulness of this data when human reviewers disagree. Expert-driven modeling offers a way to mitigate this subjectivity by incorporating expert input, which can equate to thousands of hours of video annotation. Following a video annotation process utilizing driver behavior standards, drivers' actions are categorized according to various categories and their respective frequencies recorded. This dataset has multiple applications - it can be utilized for inferring driving conditions from driver behavior scores, as external driving conditions as objects can be predicted using machine learning and have a correlation with them. A time series forecasting model also validated the dataset's efficacy by demonstrating accuracy improvements, with up to 0.24 in MAE and 0.32 in MAE, across distinct driving conditions. This dataset and associated model have been released publicly for reference at https://github.com/ExpertDB.

Despite notable progress in scene text recognition, tasks often remain hindered by a significant issue - out-of-vocabulary words that don't fit within existing training datasets. These out-of-vocabulary words can significantly hinder model accuracy and consequently affect the overall precision of these systems. In a bid to address this challenge, researchers created a new English out-of-vocabulary dataset by compiling a selection of words known to appear in street scene images but not within the Sim10k, SynthText, and GTRSB datasets commonly used for scene text recognition training. This new dataset not only fills a significant knowledge gap but also allows for the exploration of a more realistic challenge to precision. In a related development, researchers conducted an array of experiments that tested the effectiveness of various models, including synthetic and real-word extensions, as well as language model support, against the new dataset. These experiments revealed that models that leveraged real-word extensions, including the expansion of existing training datasets with additional images, and models that leveraged language model support, were able to achieve significant precision improvements when trained against the new dataset. In a related development, researchers noted a significant spike in the precision of models when the language model probability threshold was set to 1 for the OOV dataset. These findings highlighted the significant role that real-word extensions and language model support could play in further improving the precision of models against realistic out-of-vocabulary word challenges.
