We validate our model's relevance through an experimental design that tests how the shift in focus affects an investor's appetite for risk, as well as the impact of relative wealth on that appetite when absolutely wealthy and when close to being poor.

Green Pea galaxies, observed in near ultraviolet light, exhibit compact sizes and
high surface brightness, their properties moderated by gas metallicity and dust
absorption. This paper contributes to an ongoing discussion regarding the similarity
between local Green Pea galaxies and their younger, blue counterparts, which
emerge as galaxies break apart and form. Certain local Green Pea galaxies possess
the characteristics of young galaxies, balanced between star-forming activity and
supernova explosions, their properties analogues to those of their younger
counterparts, which break apart through interactions with larger galaxies.
Furthermore, the similarity between local and young Green Pea galaxies, which
emerge as galaxies break apart, highlights its significance in understanding the
cosmological volume survey programs, which aim to find and study the similar
local and young galaxies, which appear as galaxies break apart to form.

The research explores the behavior of fermions interacting with a bosonic field in different dimensions and types of materials, representing a complex system of quasiparticles. The underlying lattice is accounted for in a general way, and by using functional derivatives, it examines the effects of external influences on this interaction. The results can be applied to various systems, including superconductors, superfluids, and other complex materials. The model can also be modified to study the effects of fluctuations in density and/or magnetic field variations, and by using renormalized perturbation theory, it expands upon the Higgs model, describing how a vacuum value arises from a non-zero expectation value. The research specifically looks at the effects of fermion-boson interaction on bound-state approaches to the Higgs and Anderson transitions, and though it assumes a linear relationship between these two phenomena, it does not discuss the extent to which they co-occur.

We demonstrate that all the braided Thompson's groups exhibit linear divergence and establish that the braided groupoids associated with their right-hand sides are vast and uncontrollable. Moreover, the braided groups $G^1_r$ and $G^2_r$ are found to be inherently incoherent within their respective braided categories.

Research has shown that a combination of large memory-based retrieval and language-based generation systems can achieve exceptional performance on tasks such as natural language inference and fact-based reasoning, given access to a substantial dataset. To take advantage of this, we enhance the Retrieval Augment Generation architecture by addressing two key challenges: perfect accuracy dependence on dataset size and the limitations of embedding space. We reduce the influence of dataset size on accuracy by implementing a robust retrieval system. To mitigate the drawbacks of memory-based retrieval and improve generalization, we leverage the properties of graph data structures in an edge-indexed nearest neighbors approach. To expand the scope of the model's embeddings, we develop a novel language learning strategy that utilizes a soft-learning objective. We validate the efficacy of our enhanced architecture through our analysis of the results of a dataset shared during the Workshop on Evaluating and Analysing Self-supervised Pretraining for NLP at NeurIPS 2021.

This expository piece highlights the Riemann-Hilbert methods, a group of techniques that use Partial Differential Equations in conjunction with Analytic Function Theory, as explored within the research paper "Asymptotics of Discrete Multiple Scattering," which addresses the asymptotics of complex functions in the context of scattered poles. Specifically, the presentation focuses on the fundamental principles of the RH methods as foundational approaches to understanding asymptotic behaviors and incorporates an illustration of the methods in the context of the mentioned research paper. This exposition delves into the STF transform, the Gelfand-Division algorithm, the RH norms, and the RH methods, providing a recognized framework from the literature but applying it to the specific case of the RH basis from the mentioned research paper. This approach yields a new result which captures the long-time behavior of multiple scattering, enabled by analyzing two distinct RH problems that capture the linear independence of the STF transforms of the basis functions.

This paper presents a comprehensive approach to building a pipeline for qualifying annotations in large datasets, focusing on a specific task such as automatic summarization. Since human-generated summaries are crucial for training summarization models, a systematic method is proposed to evaluate qualification skills via a series of tests, selecting only exceptional annotators. Furthermore, a pipeline is demonstrated to utilize these qualified annotators' expertise to produce top-notch summaries, leveraging the annotators' qualitative abilities to achieve superior performance benchmarks. Interestingly, the findings show that the combination of excellent and average annotators yields comparable results to using only highly qualified annotators for summary generation. Finally, the study highlights the benefits of expert-driven annotation in summarization and the effectiveness of the qualification pipeline in achieving high-quality datasets.

Current text-video retrieval systems primarily focus on static video embeddings
that neglects the significance of spatial and temporal details within videos.
To rectify this, our proposed approach, TS2-Net, enables the production of
high-quality spatial and temporal video embeddings by effectively merging spatial
and temporal details with the aid of a contrastive learning technique. The
output from TS2-Net can then be considered suitable for use in text-video
retrieval applications and has proven its efficiency on a range of datasets,
including MS MARCO, MS COCO, and VATEX, by consistently outperforming the
current state-of-the-art models.

New research explores the connection between the LHC's rare top decays and complex Higgs models, particularly those with increased spatial dimensions. To achieve this, we first review the underlying theoretical concepts involving top quark derivatives and specialized amplitudes, followed by a detailed examination of top quark events within the standard model and their simulated outcomes, as evidenced by past studies.  Next, we delved into two novel channels from single top quark events that may appear at the LHC, providing theoretical justifications and quantitative expectations for these phenomena. These investigations enhance our understanding of new physics theories involving top quarks and multi-dimensional Higgs models, thus empowering researchers to implement more effective searches for these theories at the LHC.

A random hybrid network is created within a specified generation by connecting a certain number of vertices to an existing network.  The degree of a vertex's incoming or outgoing connections are drawn from a Poisson distribution.  The parameters of this distribution are influenced by the average degrees of the network's vertices.  We found that the degree distributions of hybrid networks and networks created through pure preferential attachment share similarities for early generations.  However, there are significant differences in the degree distributions of hybrid networks and networks created through pure preferential attachment in later generations.  The sum of the probability of a vertex's incoming or outgoing connections being zero in a hybrid network is greater than in a network created through pure preferential attachment.  We observed that vertices in early generations of a hybrid network with non-zero degrees tend to have fewer incoming or outgoing connections than vertices in a network created through pure preferential attachment, and tend to have fewer incoming or outgoing connections than vertices in later generations of a hybrid network.  We found that a vertex in a hybrid network is more likely to be connected to other vertices through indirect paths than a vertex in a network created through pure preferential attachment.  The average depth of a vertex's connections in a hybrid network is greater than in a network created through pure preferential attachment.  We found that a hybrid network shares some characteristics with hierarchical, scale-free, and random networks, and tend to be more similar to a hybrid network than a network created through pure preferential attachment or random networks

In the context of Internet of Things (IoT), various technologies like Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) and Zigbee will share the same 2 GHz frequency band, resulting in either same-technology or cross-technology interference scenarios. This research focuses on distinguishing BLE signals from two other wireless signals: Zigbee and Wi-Fi. To achieve this, we first extract features from time-domain BLE samples, then use machine learning algorithms to classify the signals. Our results indicate that signal classification accuracy can reach 95%, but note that our method is effective mainly against Zigbee, achieving only 8% accuracy when faced with Wi-Fi interference. This suggests that our method is primarily a cross-technology interference detector for BLE in 2 GHz frequencies. Furthermore, we found that enhancing the training set significantly improves the accuracy of signal classification when faced with Wi-Fi interference, albeit slightly. Finally, our method exhibits high robustness to network interference, demonstrating that it can operate effectively in challenging real-world environments.

This article explores the quantum-mechanical properties of the Klein-Gordon (KG) equation in a two-dimensional complex semi-symmetric space, which exhibits certain spacetime characteristics not found in the Minkowski framework. A novel approach is developed to analyze KG-particles in this distinctive spacetime, distinct from the Minkowski model. The article's conclusions reveal that, in this unique spacetime, KG-particles yield new concepts arise due to the gravitational influence, yielding a maximum zero-point energy. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that, in this spacetime, KG-particles display a decoupled behavior when both mass and charge are present, a distinct difference from the Minkowski model. These findings unveil the distinct quantum characteristics of the system under investigation.

It's well-known that every countable locally standard measure algebra R can be parameterized with a minimal real number $\lambda$ such that three specific sets, namely, $A_\lambda, B_\lambda, $ and $ A_\lambda \cap B_\lambda$, are measured with values greater than $\lambda$. This research aims to revisit a 1974 claim by Luschny that these algebras can also be characterized by $\lambda < \frac{1}{2}$, and as a result of our study, we achieve a stronger conclusion that $\lambda \leq \frac{1}{3}$, in addition to discovering new information about the properties of $\lambda$.

The process of extracting parton distribution E through Compton scattering is extremely challenging due to the large uncertainty in the electroweak form factor $F_{1perp}$, especially in fixed target experiments. The twist-2 even operator off-shellness $\kappa^2$ plays a crucial role in this measurement. Our research focuses on the effect of the twist-3 correction on the electroweak form factor $F_{1perp}$ and how it affects parton distribution E. We used analytical boilder calculations for twist-3 corrections and found that when calculating $E$ using the twist-3 correction, it primarily depends on the twist-3 process $g_{perp \perp}$ and on the even twist-2 process $g_{0}$ with a relative correction of approximately 30%. Our calculation also showed that the twist-3 correction turns the parton distribution E's monopole behavior into a dipole one. The maximum effect of the twist-3 correction occurs when $\kappa^2$ is approximately -0.2 GeV$^2$.

The vast majority of current large-scale AI systems rely heavily on linear classification systems due to their high efficiency and practical results. As a result, there is a pressing need to develop a quantitative concept of error correction limited to linear systems, which can bridge the gap between computational complexity theory and high-dimensional learning methods. To address this, we focus on the error correction capacity of linear classifiers, defining them within high-dimensional Euclidean spaces. Utilizing a Gaussian mixture model approach, we establish a probabilistic model for linear classifiers and determine the threshold radius for the set on which linear classifiers are perfectly accurate. Moreover, we estimate the probability that a random classifier within this radius deviates from perfection as a function of dimensionality. Specifically, we demonstrate that this probability declines exponentially on the logarithmic scale of dimensionality for classifiers close to perfect accuracy. Through an intuitive representation, we show that this model yields an effective error correction capacity for linear classifiers. Our findings also encompass the scenario of linear regression error correction. Besides providing practical estimates, our study uncovers a complex relationship between error correction and the asymptotic behavior of probabilistic mechanisms.

A spin-orbit coupled Bose-Hubbard model with distinct species exhibiting explicit symmetry and spin-orbit interactions is studied within the multi-species spinor condensate framework. By incorporating the Zeeman field into the Hamiltonian, the model reveals a rich phase diagram that includes one-dimensional superfluids with polarized and symmetric phases, as well as a quantum phase disordered state. Furthermore, in the absence of spin-orbit coupling, the model demonstrates a well-known insulating phase. The emergence of a peculiar quantum phase disordered state in one-dimensional superfluids is a previously unexplored phenomenon that contrasts with the known behavior in higher dimensions. The phase diagram also reveals a wider occurrence of superfluid phases with spinor structure and polar states. The study also examines how hopping entropy changes based on the spin-orbit coupling strength and finds that it reaches a maximum and minimum in the superfluid and quantum phase disordered states, respectively. The role of an additional inter-species interaction in modulating the phase diagram and the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and tunneling is also explored and shows that it may be possible to create a pair of separate s-wave condensates linked by a spinor bridge. The study demonstrates that spin-orbit coupling plays a significant role in quantum physics and can result in novel states of matter that differ from the known insulating and superfluid phases, particularly in one-dimensional systems.

The study proposes a universal method for determining the finite abelian p^r-group representations through a sequence of saturated Young diagram chains. It also outlines specific computation procedures for obtaining the group representations in two main categories: the Araki-Kane group representations, known for incorporating negative parts, and the Kac-Vergne group representations, recognized for their association with the coadjoint orbit U(2,2). Araki-Kane group representations can be computed directly using the diagram-based method, whereas Kac-Vergne group representations require a two-step process involving the construction and normalization of the generalized Schur functions.

Surface and line defects within gauge theory are represented as surface and line integrals in the corresponding anti-de Sitter space/two-dimensional conformal field theory scenario. Building upon previous research regarding surface and line defects in four-dimensional conformal gauge theory, we introduce novel surface and line defects along with corresponding dual operators and field theories in three and four spatial dimensions. These involve a dimension-two operator in three-dimensional conformal field theory and dimension-one operators in three and four-dimensional theories. Specifically, our focus is on a three-dimensional field theory with a U(1) symmetry and these new operators can be related to AdS magnetic and electric field configurations, respectively.

We introduce Kernel Tree, a novel machine learning model that effectively represents data properties and patterns through a tree structure. By naturally incorporating both linear and non-linear characteristics, Kernel Tree efficiently models complex relationships within the data. Its optimization capabilities are comparable to traditional kernel methods, and it can be trained under a soft constraint. Moreover, Kernel Tree's tree representation facilitates the interpretation of data patterns and characteristics in an interpretable manner. Experimental results show that Kernel Tree surpasses existing models on various regression and classification tasks, while its feature importance scores provide valuable insights into the underlying data.

A muon collider is being considered as one of the primary options for the future high-energy physics research. However, one of the main concerns for the detector design is the effect of in-flight muon decay. In this research, we present the findings of a study on the characteristics of these decays and develop a mathematical model to simulate their impact on a detector. Additionally, we propose several design modifications for the detector to minimize the negative effects of these decays, including placing muon producers and collimators at specific angles to redirect most of the muons into a recycling system for further study before they lose too much energy. We also suggest utilizing materials with high photon penetration to increase the detector's lifetime.

A new approach for efficiently training sparse neural networks, called Spartan, is presented. It effectively balances the need to explore possible solutions versus relying on already identified good configurations through a combination of random and guided searches. Spartan uses a temperature schedule to control the trade-off between exploration and exploitation, and employs an adaptive mechanism to adjust the sampling distribution towards more promising regions as it gains experience. We evaluate the efficacy of Spartan by comparing its performance with existing methods on a variety of tasks, including classifying MNIST images and processing the CIFAR10 dataset. Spartan surpasses the best available alternative by achieving significant sparsity levels of 73% and 65%, respectively. Furthermore, its ability to discover more sparse yet equally effective subnetworks with much smaller sample sizes demonstrates its superior capabilities.

To study the dynamics of a three-dimensional bosonic gas under strong interaction, we incorporate the effects of Pauli blocking in the extended Hubbard model. Through a self-consistent approach, we derive self-consistent equations for the system's mean values, then utilize the Density-Matrix Renormalization Group method to solve the model within a realistic finite box and determine the system's phase structure from the total energy. Our results show that at zero temperature, the system's phase diagram exhibits distinct first-order phase transitions at interaction strengths below the critical temperature. Furthermore, we observe the emergence of quasi-periodic semi-conducting patterns and disordered phases, and analyze the impact of boundary effects on the system's excitations, identifying finite-size effects and identifying the most probable momentum states among the system's excitations for the normal phase.

Our study explores how software developers perceive test smells in their test code, 
the severity of these smells, and any consequences including impact on project maintainability.
We conducted an online survey among 2,700 active software developers and gathered 302 responses, 
yielding 1,519 valid ratings for 25 test smells across four categories.
Our analysis shows that the severity of each smell varies greatly in terms of impact 
and maintainability impact, with some smells being perceived as having no negative effect.
Our findings highlight significant differences in how developers rate test smells 
when they are familiar with them versus when they are unaware.
We demonstrate the practical application of our research results by addressing 
common questions received from participants and suggest future studies to further investigate 
these concepts including the effectiveness of guide-lined improvement efforts.

This study investigates and analyzes a specific type of process known as an integro-differential sweeping process, which involves moving objects that interact with obstacles in higher-dimensional space. Our main finding is that the solution to this process exhibits continuity with respect to its initial conditions, especially when these conditions involve objects from sweeping processes. To further expand our work, we present two additional outcomes: Firstly, we demonstrate that the solution to the closed-loop system formed by integrating the control process is continuous. Secondly, using the differentiability of the solution from a previous research study as a starting point, we prove the existence of a locally Lipschitz solution.

A enhanced Monte Carlo algorithm for the interaction of $e^+e^-$ physics has been developed and its precision in predicting various observables has been evaluated for several $e^+e^-$ collision processes. By utilizing the ADAMS framework for the evaluation of integrals, significant speed increases have been achieved without sacrificing the accuracy of the predictions made by its predecessor, the SMC sample file. On average, the predictions made by the updated algorithm are more precise than those made by the original, exhibiting an improvement of approximately one order of magnitude. This updated tool is now available for download at https://github.com/ph-ed/SMCee.

Deep learning techniques have improved pressure waveform beat intervals extraction from noisy signals, but have not been applied to electrocardiograms (ECGs) despite being superior to traditional methods. We developed a two-stage approach using a deep learning algorithm to improve inter-beat interval extraction from ECGs by first beating noise with a deep learning denoising method and then employing another denoising method to improve ECG quality. The inter-beat intervals were then extracted using a time series analysis technique. The proposed approach's performance was evaluated using ECGs from individuals with and without diabetes. The results demonstrated that our approach outperformed the exogenous interval extraction technique by maintaining better ECG quality while reducing errors. Conversely, our approach's implicit interval extraction method excelled the exogenous technique by achieving a lower root mean square error. The implicit method's error was on par with the exogenous method but significantly outperformed it when the ECG was poor.

This research introduces a randomized algorithm for computing the singular value decomposition (sVD) of a third-order tensor, referred to as t-SVD. We demonstrate that our method achieves optimal performance in terms of the number of data tensor passes, comparable to the best existing algorithms. Additionally, we showcase the applicability of this approach to the computation of a color image's singular value decomposition. Through our analysis, we establish a guarantee for the approximate subspace of the top singular subspaces. We also modify the algorithm to efficiently compute a low-rank approximation of a tensor, and the guarantee extends to this rank approximation. We conduct experiments that validate our method's performance, assessing its accuracy and dimension-finding capabilities. We find that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly when determining singular dimensions, which it does efficiently.

Despite the effectiveness of static graph representation learning, dynamic graph embedding poses significant challenges and presents novel opportunities. This area of research focuses on modeling changing graph structures over time. This Real-Time Embedding of Dynamic Graphs (RTE-DG) survey covers recent developments in representing temporal graphs. It highlights distinct approaches to accounting for the evolving edge structures of dynamic networks versus those focusing on nodal relationships. Additionally, the survey highlights evolving scenarios in which graphs are observed (temporal, sensory, computational) and compares static graph partitioning methods with those applicable to dynamic graphs. Finally, the survey touches on the interplay between temporal graph embedding and prediction tasks within dynamic systems.

Our studies of $^7$H resonances have revealed the presence of a single, narrow low-energy resonance at approximately 64 keV above the proton-separation threshold in the $^8$He system. This finding is supported by both the $^7$H + 2N and $^8$He + N scattering models. Notably, the observed width of about 8 keV is significantly narrower than the predicted ground-state width of approximately 19 keV for the 64 keV resonance at N$^{2+}$ channel. We observed an unbound state in the $^8$He system with a 2N separation energy of about 92 keV, which is close to the $^8$He + 2N threshold energy. The predicted ground-state width in the N$^{2+}$ channel for this 92 keV resonance is approximately 28 keV, which is substantially larger than the observed width of about 13 keV. Our statistical and dynamical models provide insights into the quadrupole asymmetry and statistical potential of the $^8$He system, ultimately contributing to the understanding of superasymptotic tunneling in the $^7$H valley.

This paper focuses on a Nirenberg-type problem defined on the surface of a dimensional sphere at its halfway point.  For the critical dimension at hand, it is determined via variational methods that the most extreme solutions exhibit the same multiplicity in their points of inflection as on the full dimensional sphere, but distinctly, these points of inflection never converge towards the boundary. Moreover, for subcritical dimensions, no bounded extreme solutions exist; an alternate solution approach using blowout techniques reveals the existence of an infinite number of critical solutions featuring a specific multiplicity of points of inflection. Our approach to solving the problem is linked to an earlier, more conventional method that employs blowout techniques in a Nirenberg-type problem defined on the full dimensional sphere, but distinctly, these points of inflection never converge towards the boundary.

For unsupervised clustering in large datasets, the goal is to determine the optimal number of clusters. We present an innovative deep learning approach called Deep Class-wise Discrepancy Loss (DCDL) that results in more distinct feature representations for its class-wise applicability. DCDL clustering methodology starts with training a clustering model using all dataset examples, followed by applying a different loss function, DCDL, during a secondary fine-tuning process. DCDD utilizes class information to minimize feature differences within each cluster while maximizing differences between clusters, achieving more pronounced feature separation. Experiments on four benchmark datasets reveal that incorporating DCDD yields superior results, particularly for challenging small-scale clustering tasks, by further enhancing the distinction in feature spaces learned by state-of-the-art clustering models. Notably, our method is the first to apply class-wise loss functions for clustering tasks.

To gauge the impact of local tracing initiatives in England's COVID-19 test and trace program, a two-step evaluation approach is employed. Firstly, a detailed examination of the program's implementation, including its organizational structure, data collection methods, and workflow dynamics, is carried out. This informs a realistic, simulation-based analysis to assess the program's efficacy under various scenarios. Our analysis shows that partnering with local tracing services doesn't substantially enhance the overall efficiency of the test and trace program but does provide a notable performance improvement in specific low-prevalence areas due to reduced workload. Nonetheless, this gain is likely overshadowed by the program's failure to leverage the local tracing partnerships' unique strengths, such as enhanced community engagement and targeted contact tracing efforts. Moreover, our study highlights the program's vulnerability to excessive workloads within the test and trace system.

Located at approximately 1 kpc, Melotte 72 is one of the closest star clusters to the Sun, being only shy of 20 degrees from the Sun's disc. The cluster's age has been a subject of interest, with estimates ranging from around 320 to 700 million years. Recent studies have primarily focused on the photometric development of the cluster's younger, 320 million-year-old B-star population. Our research aims to refine the age of Melotte 72 by utilizing Gaia DR2 data containing about 420,000 sources within the cluster's boundaries. Using Gaia's parallax and proper motion data, along with colour-magnitude analysis of the cluster's main-sequence, we've established an age of around 540 million years. During this process, our calculations revealed that the solar nebula's metal content is comparable to the Sun's, providing further validation point for our findings. Melotte 72 is estimated to have formed approximately 160 million years after the formation of the Hyades and approximately 320 million years prior to the formation of the Pleiades. The latter estimate aligns with prior studies, while our current results provide a more accurate timeframe for the former. Melotte 72 is estimated to live for around 420 million years, making it one of the longer-lived star clusters of its age group. Our research also indicates that the Gaia data allows for precise estimation of the cluster's main-sequence turn-off mass at around 2.

We investigate the behavior of the two-dimensional random field $X$ on unit squares $\mathbb{R}^2 \,/\, [0,1]^2$ as it undergoes a phase transition in its excursion levels. Specifically, we analyze a random field defined by integrating a standard two-dimensional Gaussian field, $Z$, which is restricted to a version of the unit square with a cutout segment removed. The phase transition occurs when the length of the cutout segment varies, specifically when it approaches zero from the left and zero from the right, at which point the excursion levels of $X$ experience a sharp transition in distribution. Notably, this phase transition is characterized by the occurrence of an 'order-disorder' transition, epitomized by the shifting from a pattern-rich Gaussian to a pattern-less Gaussian behavior, which is exemplified by the transition from the two-dimensional Gaussian field $Z$ to the one-dimensional Gaussian field $X_1$ modulo 1.

This study presents a novel approach to directional light source calibration in 2D, applying it to an autonomous driving dataset. A comprehensive comparison of direct regression versus traditional methods revealed significant time savings, up to 6 times faster, when using the proposed direct regression approach. Notably, the results also indicated that fewer images are required to achieve accurate calibration when employing direct regression. A further investigation explored the impact of varying light source orientations and included an in-depth analysis of a hypothetical scenario with perpendicular light sources. Ultimately, the results show that direct regression is a more efficient and reliable method for directional light source calibration. A publicly available implementation can be accessed via the repository https://github.com/0rox/dls_calibrated_cameras.

Agents acting in environments can develop learned constraints that are based on the rules governing their behavior. This concept of constraints can be useful for reinforcement learning settings, where agents can learn to adhere to specific rules leading to desired behaviors. A novel approach to this idea involves learning constraints experimentally, through non-technical methods employed by experts, using a gesture recognition system. Expert operators use a hand-gesture system to enforce rules, which is then translated into reinforcement learning-style constraints, using a hand-gesture encoder. This implementation allows for several useful applications, including the combination of human and robotic skills and the safety feature that prevents agents from carrying out dangerous actions.

The GAIA space mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) is a groundbreaking asset for determining the positions, distances, movements, and other characteristics of the stars within our galaxy, and for studying their patterns of motion. Launched in 2015, GAIA has collected an immense amount of data, which has been thoroughly analyzed and published in the GAIA Data Release 3 (DR3). This release contains comprehensive Gaia-based stellar information (parallax, proper motion, photometry, and spectral analysis data) along with additional external datasets (e-WISE and VVV surveys). This chapter delimits the applicable mathematical domains (parallax-pulse, proper motion-pulse, colour-magnitude diagrams) and spatial boundaries (Galactic coordinates, distance from the galactic plane) of the GAIA Data Release 3 (DR3). These limitations take into consideration factors such as noise, systematic errors, and completeness gaps as well as physical constraints (i.e., the laws of physics). This work draws upon prior similar studies (e.g., : Sartore et al. 2016 ; Lattanzi & Boschi 2019 ; Vallenari et al. 2017 ; Cuby et al. 2019 ; Lattanzi & Bonoli 2018 ; Bonito et al. 2019 ; Loppeni et al. 2019 ; Reino et al. 2018 ; Loppeni et al. 201

Trees that describe the structure of graphs serve as a crucial algorithmic tool. Researchers have hitherto mainly employed tree decompositions for graph analysis. This paper introduces a novel method of representing graphs through trees, referred to as the NP-tree, which inherently encodes various graph Clauses. We demonstrate that by exploiting the inherent connection between NP-trees and Clauses, we can efficiently solve key classical graph problems such as Vertex Cover and MaxCut on bounded treewidth graphs much faster. Specifically, the time complexity of these problems is directly proportional to a small constant power of the variable count, a substantial improvement over the existing time complexity of these problems. Moreover, this advancement is further underscored by a lower bound on the complexity of approximating these problems, showing that our algorithm is near-optimal in terms of performance.

Researchers have developed a variety of graph clustering (community detection) methods, ranging from sophisticated models with complex optimization processes to simple, yet effective approaches like the Zhang--Horvath clustering. This latter method, which is a continuous graph clustering based on the nearest neighbor definition, has been previously overlooked in the field. In contrast, our proposed continuous clustering coefficient is sensitive to optimization methods and network generation models, resulting in distinct behaviors and performance outcomes. While both metrics share similarities, we observe that the Zhang--Horvath clustering exhibits a more dependent relationship with the underlying network and employs a coarser detection process. Furthermore, our results indicate that for certain networks, the proposed continuous clustering, which accounts for the degree of nodes, surpasses the Zhang--Horvath clustering in numerous settings. In light of these findings, we contend that the Zhang--Horvath clustering should be regarded as a special case of the proposed continuous clustering, rather than an alternative metric.

A proposed method for error assessment and prediction certainty certification in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) relies on the reliance of numerical solutions on approximate models. By utilizing a posteriori error estimation, PINNs' confidence in predicting solutions to differential equations with uncertain parameters can be evaluated. This approach develops a framework for certifying predictions by leveraging the accuracy of numerical solutions generated from the PINNs. By utilizing a constructed reliable subsolution, this method facilitates the derivation of a rigorous bound on the solution range, effectively extending the existing work on robust optimization to approximate models. Experimental results obtained using the proposed approach for identifying unknown parameter values in differential equations with uncertain parameters show promising potential for its extension to predicting uncertain output values.

Spatial dependency models have become fundamental components in the creation and analysis of air pollution models. Past research has established the development and assessment of these models using observational data, focusing primarily on autocorrelation measures and spatial regression. Recent breakthroughs in spatial statistics have introduced more efficient methods for spatial model estimation and prediction, particularly the use of Gaussian process emulators. This study proposes the use of backfit, a novel approach to detecting spatial non-stationarity and evaluating spatial covariance models. Backfit analyzes residuals derived from hierarchical generalized linear models, then applies a multi-scale empirical kernel to study the spatial pattern at different levels. By considering the influence of wind direction and speed, backfit adds a non-stationary factor to demonstrate the presence of spatial non-stationarity. Backfit's performance was tested using simulated data and real-world air pollution data from Los Angeles and New York City, revealing significant spatial non-stationarity in these real-world cases and identifying distinct scales of variability.

The non-topological supergauge theory with a massless fermion in 1+1 dimensions exhibits a double zero-energy peak in the real-space Andreev spectrum, a feature not influenced by non-Majorana effects. Conversely, the theoretical model shows that this zero-energy peak can withstand non-Majorana-related influences and double zero-energy peaks. Conversely, the theoretical model indicates that this zero-energy peak can withstand non-Majorana-related influences and doubles under temperature variations. Specifically, the theoretical model reveals that the Andreev spectrum evolves according to a temperature-dependent, symmetrical curve as the temperature increases towards the Fermi energy, with the latter serving as a transitional point. Below the Fermi energy, the theoretical model identifies two distinct peaks - zero-energy and Fermi-energy peaks - with the former being twice larger than the latter at zero Kelvin. Conversely, the Fermi-energy peak doubles in size while the zero-energy peak disappears as the temperature increases towards the Fermi energy.

This research investigates the spectral characteristics of linear bandit models and introduces a model selection method that is spectrally grounded. From this approach, we derive both model selection and clustering results for linear bandit models, yielding tighter lower and upper bounds than existing least-squares alternatives. Specifically, our spectral clustering outcome produces a sharper minimax bound than the traditional least-squares method. Moreover, we apply this framework to identify both general and sparsity-level assumptions for kernelized, linear, and contextual bandit models. Importantly, our spectral clustering achieves a sharper minimax bound for Seeger's kernelized linear bandit model than previous kernel-ridge least-squares results. Finally, we retain statistical query complexity insights from previous research to provide additional model selection results for linear bandit frameworks.

In systems with lattice symmetry, valley and orbital properties become interconnected, with the two being measured using the same parameter - conductivity. However, in a triangular lattice, applying a magnetic field only controls the orbitals, making the valley Hall effect ambiguous. This is where the orbital Hall effect comes in, offering a clearer measurement. To take advantage of this, researchers have created a device combining graphene and a SrTiO3 wafer with engineered oxygen vacancies, which exhibit not only Hall conductivity but also a new type of transport characterized by superionic conductivity.

Recent research employs Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods to address adversarial machine learning (AdML) tactics, typically training agents in an adversarial environment to counter attacks using evolutionary algorithms similar to direct gradient optimization. Nonetheless, all existing RL-based solutions lack a adversarial finding mechanism, relying on pre-set exploration scenarios to discover adversarial strategies. Moreover, all current RL training, including evaluation, operates within the same environment as the trained agent, thus suffering from the limitations of in-sample optimization, lacking generalizability to unseen scenarios. This paper introduces a novel framework, called FedEmpower, which addresses these issues using federated learning and genetic reinforcement learning to boost the capability of neural networks against adversarial attacks across various scenarios, including generative and black-box attacks, without relying on prior knowledge and without the need for simultaneous training and testing within the same environment. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this framework against adversarial attacks and demonstrate its ability to discover effective countermeasures on two benchmark datasets, CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet. Our framework is open-source and can be accessed at https://github.com/FV-EC-Lab/FedEmpower.

In problems such as finding analogs to celestial sources, growing sets of mathematical models, or matching textual descriptions, a similar choice must be made repeatedly. Determining how much weight to give each choice can be crucial. Past attempts often relied on the past stability of the choices or using the choices' expected values, which are less relevant once the choices' distribution has shifted. This paper presents a new approach called Stochastic Sequential Estimation Using Temporal Means, which makes the most of the statistical trends in the previous choices. It does this by incorporating the means of the choices into a decision-making process, which is shown to significantly improve the outcome. This method is tested with a number of designs, including finding similar celestial sources and matching textual descriptions. The results show that this approach far outperforms previous methods when the choices' distribution has changed the most. Includes a supplemental journal article with figures and tables.

We plan to establish that for any set of cardinals $\{ \mathfrak{m}_i \}_{i \in I}$, which may be uncountable, the following statement holds: The class of ordinals with a cardinality of $\mathfrak{m}_i$ is not stationary for all $i \in I$. This will be achieved by a different method than in the case where the number of cardinals in the set is countable. Furthermore, we aim to prove that the $C\dot{o}cean principle$ implies the $club filter's$ property of $S-incompleteness$.

Current visualisation tools for concept ontologies are simple and non-interactive, making it difficult to thoroughly examine complex relationships.  As a result, researchers have limited insight into the structures of their data.  As an improvement, OntoPlot is a more advanced, interactive visualisation tool that provides two-dimensional layouts of concept ontologies, enabling the detection of highly connected concepts.  Its interactive function enables users to gain a rapid, overall understanding of the intricate links within the data.  A case study was conducted to test OntoPlot's effectiveness by comparing its visualisations to those produced by the existing non-interactive tool, Power Plot,  using medical and electrical engineering ontologies.  A user study demonstrated that OntoPlot is preferred over Power Plot and that it is an effective tool for learning about concept ontologies.

Our proposed method integrates CycleGAN and SelfSupervisedLearning (SSSL) for unsupervised cross-domain image translation tasks while maintaining the original characteristics of input features. The cycle-consistent cycle-loss in CycleGAN ensures that the images after domain transformation can return to the original form, thereby preventing property loss during domain translation. However, this loss primarily focuses on minimizing the difference between images after domain translation and those in the original form, and it doesn't have a direct constraint on maintaining the original characteristics. On the other hand, contrastive loss in SSSL facilitates compact feature learning by pushing feature embeddings from images across domains towards negative feature embeddings. However, this loss can't guarantee that the feature embeddings of images before and after domain translation are the same. To address these issues, we suggest using CycleGAN together with contrastive loss and feature variation loss to form a new cycle-consistent contrastive loss. This loss allows for cycle-contrastive learning that maintains the original characteristics of images during domain translation. As a result, when applied to three cross-domain image translation tasks namely, building-frametransfer, face-domain-transfer, and face-synthesizability, our method significantly outperforms baseline techniques. Specifically, our code can be found at: https://github.com/asharakee/Cycle-Contrastive

Generative models have effectively created realistic data, but their performance has been limited when dealing with complex, semi-realistic data due to inadequate density models. New advances in deep learning now enable generative models to create versatile, high-quality sound files and audio sequences directly from raw audio, opening up new possibilities for integrating generative and non-generative models to create hybrid approaches. This research achieves a milestone by developing a hybrid method that combines a neural score estimator and a neural audio synthesizer to generate highly realistic music scores and audio sequences simultaneously. This method leverages the strength of two existing deep learning models, demonstrating the potential for future integration with other generative models to create advanced audio generators. Experimental results indicate that our approach surpasses existing non-generative methods in score prediction and outperforms a leading deep learning model in audio generation, producing highly realistic results that maintain structural and statistical consistency with real music. By blending generative and non-generative models, we demonstrate a robust and versatile method that can be successfully applied to a wide range of tasks, including music synthesis, instrument modeling, and score-inversion. Additionally, we create a dataset with extensive multitrack annotations for the music domain, enabling future research in audio technology to utilize this dataset for reference.

The temperature-dependent movement of gases and fluids is influenced by their molecular structure and flexibility, which and is captured in the thermal diffusion factor. Currently, classical models are unable to accurately predict this phenomenon. However, a new quantum mechanical method has demonstrated improved results, particularly for binary mixtures with complex properties. Its effectiveness has been successfully tested across a range of different molecules and fluid combinations. Its prediction accuracy exceeds that of classical models, particularly for mixtures of gases with flexible molecules. It's worth noting that quantum effects are more likely to manifest at lower temperatures. Therefore, quantum mechanics may need to be considered in evaluating the efficiency of quantum-based models.

Recent research into transformer-based models for natural language processing has heavily focused on their pre-training. It has been observed that continually fine-tuning these models post-training leads to improved performance and reduced likelihood of overfitting. This study aims to understand how varying the number of post-training training epochs, model parameter count, and dataset size affects their overall performance. The examination, conducted using seven distinct datasets, compares the performance of eight different models, including three that utilize CNN architectures and five pre-trained transformers, such as BERT and XLNet, subject to different training scenarios. The results indicate that fine-tuned models with a relatively small number of parameters often match or exceed the performance of the larger, pre-trained transformers. The outcomes also show that the size of the dataset has a more significant impact on the model's performance than the number of training epochs. For practical application, the research suggests that developing efficient, finely-tuned models can be a viable strategy for achieving good results, and further emphasizes the importance of dataset size in achieving good performance.

We resolve the longstanding issue of unsupervised learning for box re-ranking, a problem that has been avoided in the past due to the inherent difficulty of learning a ranking function. Our approach involves converting the problem from a traditional machine learning perspective to a box re-ranking one, which we call Self-Knowledge Distillation. This innovation allows us to harness self-supervised information from features, without requiring any explicitly labeled data during model training. Our solution comprises two distinct stages: initially, we conduct a warm-up phase where we identify relatively easy passages and transform the distillation loss to focus on comparing passage scores. Subsequently, we maximize the inter-class dissimilarity between top-ranked passages while minimizing intra-class dissimilarity, which significantly enhances our model's performance. Comprehensive experiments conducted on MS MARCO Web Search DuLMv2, Colmar, and WebSearch-100 demonstrate that our approach surpasses both weakly-supervised and strong baselines by substantial margins, with our final result outperforming the top-ranked system at MSDC 2019 by 16.0% in terms of R@10 recall. Furthermore, our method achieves the best performance seen so far on Colmar by a considerable margin of 27.88% over the top-performing system. Notably, our solution functions effectively as an effective regularizer when combined with other pre-training objectives.

The prevalence of low-quality music recordings is a challenge that needs addressing. These recordings often suffer from significant issues, such as low sound quality, which compromises their value. One innovative solution to enhance low-quality music is tapping into the latest advancements in deep learning technology. Following the success of deep learning in improving audio quality, a wide range of applications has been developed that can refine various music attributes. Despite its potential, a deep learning based method to enhance low-quality music was only introduced relatively recently. Furthermore, a combined approach that utilizes both a limit-based and a generative model has not been explored for music signal processing applications. Limit-based models produce results within a predefined limit by adjusting gain, whereas generative models can produce unique outcomes by learning from data. In our research, we integrate these two models into a system that can restore multiple attributes of low-quality music simultaneously. In practical tests, our method demonstrated superior performance and produced more natural results by combining the strengths of limit-based and generative model techniques. Our experimental results also demonstrated that our method outperformed existing leading techniques, such as music information retrieval tasks involving low-bitrate MP3 compression and music noise removal. In terms of applications, our method holds promise for real-world applications, such as music from speech, music restoration, and music video compression.

This research extends previous work on hand-thrown object movement reproduction, implementing a system that allows users to control animations via hand gestures. Users input desired object poses, and the system generates more realistic motion, including rotations, via hand-thrown motion databases matching the input poses. Evaluations with architectural students revealed that integrating rotational motion made the motion appear more realistic, especially when the original input poses lacked sufficient rotational information. Although adding rotational data significantly improved perception of realistic movements in most cases, a minor adjustment to the system's process was needed to address instances of underflow errors in rotations. Based on evaluation results, a simple fix was implemented, and the system's integration into a tangible interface for interactive object manipulation was confirmed.

By integrating syntax-aware features into our attention model, we enhance both the way NMT arranges its translations and the way it decides what to translate, thereby fine-tuning its output. Experimental results demonstrate increased fluency using a fixed translation order but also revealed that current NMT systems can benefit from minimal improvements in translation order. Furthermore, our model's reliance on explicit syntax-based attention mechanisms leads to decreased translation quality when applied to the standard NMT training datasets. Nonetheless, incorporating our model along with other (source and target) syntax-based features within the NMT framework yields notable enhancements in translation quality, stemming from the added flexibility in translating uneven sentences. We also developed an unsupervised method for extracting syntax-aware attention features from NMT's sequence-based hidden states by utilizing an HMM and an alignment metric, and when used in conjunction with the original model, resulted in minimal further improvements in translation quality. Lastly, we observed that combining our attention model with varying degrees of pre-trained syntax features yields significantly better translation quality, especially when employed in transfer scenarios where source and target languages have different syntax.

Planetary formation is constrained by snow lines in protoplanetary disks, with snow-related opacity processes used to estimate these locations through theoretical modeling. Opacity-related transport mechanisms might also influence dust distribution and snow-related opacity processes. To investigate this relationship, we studied opacity-driven transport in 2D using a nonlinear diffusion equation with a Rayleigh-Taylor instability-like model. Our research reveals that turbulent flow can rapidly move snow-related opacity processes in space, potentially matching observations of dust distribution rather than theoretical snow line locations. This possibility is confirmed by analyzing data from the HL Tau disk, with differential equations modeling opacity-driven transport matching dust distribution patterns in the 0.1 mm grain sector. Opacity-driven transport could also be observed in future exoplanet direct imaging missions.

To accurately simulate a physical process using a statistical model, the parameters must be set to mirror the actual distribution of data collected from the experiment. CaloGraph5 is a comprehensive tool for both collecting mock data and refining the parameters of the caloric distribution, the latter by employing a Bayesian approach to eliminate the need for time-consuming markov chain simulations. The utility offers a range of features that facilitate the process, including an adaptive algorithm for determining the optimal number of iterations and a reliability test for assessing and establishing confidence intervals around the optimal parameters. The code, along with a detailed guide and illustrative examples, are publicly available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/lucabruno/CaloGraph5.

We introduce a quantum-inspired learning approach, which involves learning a quantum state via repeated measurements, focusing on the theoretical boundaries of what can be achieved. Firstly, we establish that the expectation values of any observables can be estimated by repeating experiments, specifically, the variance of our estimates for an observable A, is proportional to the average of the squares of its expectation values, for a specific number of experiments. Secondly, we develop a strategy to simultaneously estimate the expectation values of a set of non-commuting observables. Thirdly, we explore the minimum number of experiments necessary to reach an optimal level of precision for these estimates, demonstrating that both the precision of estimates of expectation values and the minimum number of experiments have specific limits, thereby paving the way for achieving complete state reconstruction. Finally, we examine the efficiency of our approach and consider practical implementations, as well as its practical applications, such as conducting measurements without actually measuring, and certifying the presence of specific particles, like photons.

The improved formula for the Born approximation allows for corrections to the two-term approximation of the field, generated from the spectrum of the propagator, which was initially identified by Budko, Gurevich, and Polyansky (J. By adapting this approach, we develop a novel method to compute the propagator for one-dimensional Schrödinger equations, whose spectra are not necessarily discrete and continuum states do not necessarily decrease exponentially at infinity. The method also extends to the computation of partial derivatives of the propagator, whose values at a point are represented by an integral of the propagator over a large area, using Green's formula. We've introduced two new methods, transmutations and mixture mutations that deviate from conventional one-to-one class label mappings in out-of-dimension domain adaptation challenges. The transmutation method uniquely changes class labels by preserving their original order, whereas mixture mutations blend labels without this restriction. To accommodate these unique mutations, we've developed a novel symmetric version of the Minimum Distance to Mean Class Center (MDMC) approach, which we call Symmetric MDMC (SMDMC). The SMDMC method offers a simple, symmetric approach to learning in the transformed domain. We've observed that using either transmutations or mixture mutations with SMDMC yields MDMC performance levels or even surpasses it in many cases. When applied to a variety of domain adaptation scenarios, the transmutation method produces more consistent results than methods with one-to-one label mappings and even outperforms MDMC in some cases. The method also achieves equivalent performance to mixture mutations when compared to using all class labels in the mixture.

Multi-task linear regression, with its straightforward parameterization and well-known solutions, becomes significantly more difficult when sample efficiency is considered. Sublinear sample efficiency is particularly challenging as it necessitates minimizing both individual and total least square errors using a single pass through the data. Previous solutions for sublinear sample efficiency were complex and involved quadratic programming, which necessitated solving a large number of expensive optimization problems. We propose an innovative algorithm that employs a novel, tree-based structure called an OBFT to solve the problem efficiently. With its collective and efficient pruning capability, the OBFT facilitates a more streamlined approach to solving multiple related least square errors, thus alleviating some of the computational burdens associated with quadratic programming. We demonstrate that our algorithm is highly efficient at achieving sublinear sample efficiency in multi-task linear regression models. Furthermore, the algorithm's applicability is expanded to include more complex models such as deep linear networks by introducing a new, tree-based back-propagation method. This advancement allows for efficient parameter updates in these more complex models as well. We report exceptional results from the algorithm in terms of its performance on multi-task regression and related linear bandit tasks, all achieved using a single pass through the data.

Recent years have seen an increased focus on multilingual language models, aimed at breaking free from the limitations of current singular language models. Unlike their counterparts with limited data, basic unsupervised preprocessing is often sufficient for classification tasks in highly resource-rich languages. Nevertheless, for languages with less data, such as German, Hungarian and Finnish, this is not the case, requiring more complex preprocessing. This study introduces a new, unsupervised setup for preprocessing, aiming to bring distributional similarity between train and test sets. The proposed approach, an adaptation of the DataNoising technique, is a form of post-training quantization, distinct from its application in feature extraction. The study examines its effectiveness in comparison to Knowledge Distillation, assessing its ability to develop a consistent performance across different languages. The results show that post-training quantization yields consistent results in classification for low-resource languages, maintaining performance levels similar to those achieved with Knowledge Distillation. Moreover, the study highlights the beneficial effects of post-training quantization on the model's ability to withstand data poisoning attacks, indicating its potential as a straightforward yet efficient data augmentation strategy.

To address limitations in accessing labeled data for detecting COVID-19 and pneumonia, we investigate the effectiveness of various data enhancements. Our results show that imposing specific image transformations on a small set of annotated images (only 5% of the total dataset) yields comparable performance, suggesting a significant reduction in required labeled data (-85%). This is verified by conducting experiments using multiple algorithms, including two pre-trained CNNs (DenseNet and VGG16), and two unsupervised learning methods (VAEs and an auto-encoder designed to preserve pneumonia-related image features).

We have developed a novel, scalable approach for image captioning that incorporates prompt learning. This approach embeds prompt learning within the image captioning architecture, effectively transforming it into a prompt-based learning problem. This innovation enables image captioning to leverage the extensive pre-trained language models designed for text-based tasks, thereby taking advantage of their superior language skills. Moreover, our approach simplifies the computationally intensive process of sampling diverse captions during training. This method's embedded and embedded-batch variants offer further improvements by integrating prompt learning with the attention module and batch normalization, respectively. Ultimately, our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art models in image captioning tasks, delivering enhanced performance and increased efficiency. Our code is available for download at https://github.com/zhedser/pail.

Concepts like causation and contrastive causation, which highlight what didn't happen, are crucial in various fields including science, everyday life, and philosophy. They play a significant role in understanding different types of harm, such as causation that results in an undesirable outcome or contrastive causation that increases the likelihood of an undesirable outcome. However, past philosophies have been ambiguous in describing cause-and-effect relationships, particularly in situations where making distinctions between them proves difficult or impossible. This confusion is reflected in attempts to explain utility-based harm, which includes concepts like utility loss and sacrifice, with some examples suggesting non-causal relationships and others requiring causation. We argue that looking at things from a different perspective, focusing on what didn't happen, resolves these ambiguities and reveals that all these concepts rely on contrastive causation that increases the likelihood of an undesirable outcome. This new perspective indicates that past difficulties are not only resolved but also the varied definitions of utility-based harm, such as utility loss and sacrifice, are ultimately the same. Moreover, this realisation enables us to address long-standing questions about harm that have gone unanswered before, such as the distinction between causing an actual loss of utility and merely making something else impossible, with a clear distinction between them. Moreover, this new perspective is not only applicable to utility-based harm but also enables us to understand causation leading to an undesirable outcome more clearly by differentiating it from contrastive causation that increases the likelihood of an desirable outcome. The widespread use of camera traps in wildlife conservation has led to the capture of vast wildlife images. Effective analysis of these images is crucial not only for identifying the presence of different species but also for estimating their population numbers. Recent advancements in deep learning have opened new avenues for analyzing these images, paving the way for increased automation in wildlife monitoring. This article delves into recent research on applying deep learning techniques to estimate wildlife population numbers by analyzing camera trap images. We provide a detailed overview of relevant deep learning methodologies, discuss the challenges associated with using deep learning in wildlife conservation, and explore emerging trends, such as the utilization of artificial intelligence at the edge for population estimation. Additionally, we highlight potential future research directions and embark on a discussion of potential applications of deep learning in addressing real-world challenges related to wildlife conservation.

STMT is a multilingual speech translation task that typically uses a fixed target vocabulary.
The goal of this study is to explore zero-shot STMT methods that can add new languages
to its system without retraining, thereby allowing it to handle unexpected languages in real-world applications.
To achieve this challenge, researchers proposed two approaches: one that adds new languages
to STMT using a text-to-text model with a large, multilingual vocabulary, and another
that uses a common speech-to-text model and a set of language-specific text generation models.
Both approaches were able to handle zero-shot and few-shot translation tasks more effectively.
The results from a German-to-Czech translation task, which was used as a test case, showed
that these zero-shot methods can succeed even when there is little data available for translation.
The success of these approaches suggests that zero-shot STMT is a viable option for cross-lingual speech translation in the future.

We develop non-relativistic particle and heat transport equations using the relativistic fading memory model as a foundation. These new equations extend existing Newtonian models by incorporating the memory influence seen in relativistic theory. To derive these equations from first principles, we apply the principle of minimum entropy, supporting our findings with the existence and uniqueness of global solutions and confirming that the total entropy of the system reaches its maximum value. In addition, we examine the rate of entropy growth using a relativistic entropy production bound. These new equations apply the non-Markovian fading memory concept to Newtonian models of particle and heat transport, leading to novel expressions for velocity and heat distribution in terms of the initial conditions and a non-local relativistic history. In the limit where relativistic speeds are virtually unattainable, these new equations reduce to the Newtonian models they fundamentally derive from.

Predicting energy demand at high resolution is vital for managing power distribution during peak hours. Conventional forecasting techniques, such as ARIMA and CNNs, can fall short when analyzing the patterns of peak energy usage. This limitation motivates the development of a novel deep learning approach, known as a Graph Spatial Temporal Residual Convolutional Neural Network (G-STRCNN). This method leverages historical energy data to identify emerging patterns in energy demand. Our research involves creating synthetic time series based on real-world energy data for the United States and evaluating the performance of our proposed G-STRCNN method using advanced metrics. The results show that by integrating standard energy forecasts with peak energy forecasts, G-STRCNN achieves significantly lower MAE and RMSE errors, indicating an improvement of 10% and 25%, respectively. Furthermore, the G-STRCNN method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, such as Protonedale-CNN and multi-task ARIMA-CNN models, which were previously considered superior solutions.

To effectively utilize machine learning algorithms in real-world applications, it is crucial to comprehend how they operate and make decisions. Although significant advancements have been made, algorithms today primarily rely on empirical models and data-driven methods. Incorporating knowledge from various expertise sources can enhance the performance, efficiency, and reliability of machine learning models. This knowledge transfer involves two primary strategies: (1) infusing algorithms with knowledge to maintain stability, and (2) adapting existing knowledge to accommodate new scenarios. To facilitate the implementation of knowledge utilization in machine learning, a comprehensive framework is proposed, incorporating essential components and a unified conceptual structure. This framework is then applied to two specific domains, multiple model tracking and optical flow estimation, and is demonstrated to achieve improved performance by leveraging the insights of experts in these fields. By systematically analyzing the key concepts and related research, it is hoped that this knowledge utilization framework can spur future innovations and contribute to the broader machine learning community.

We introduce an image-driven framework called Latent LeQ, which enhances the precision of preoperative lesion localization using a unique technique. Traditional localization techniques typically require detailed anatomical data or segmentations of lesions, but our method utilizes only visual information, including patient image patches and ground truth lesion labels. To overcome the scarcity of detailed anatomical data, our technique generates pseudo annotations and promotes high-quality predictions by utilizing a weighted loss function. Notably, our approach demonstrates successful localization of lesions in brain tumors, pulmonary nodules and polyps, achieving impressive localization accuracy of 87%, 85%, and 86% respectively. Our experiments demonstrate that, unlike conventional methods, Latent LeQ achieves enhanced performance on a range of medical image datasets when compared to detailed anatomical data, showcasing its effectiveness and generalizability across various modalities and diseases.

Our primary objective is to automatically identify vertebrae in spinal CT images in an accurate manner. The automatic encoding process we developed from the supervision of expert radiologists yields superior results, with 88% accuracy, significantly outperforming the best competing methods with fast computation speeds. The encoding stands at a detailed anatomical level, with distinct features for each vertebra, and we found that our method successfully distinguishes even similar vertebra characteristics. By using the experts' knowledge to guide the learning process, we found that the system generalizes effectively to different populations, and our method meets the accepted standard for manual readings in terms of sensitivity and accuracy, while also providing clear and interpretable results for human consumption.
